beats.title: The Roster
beats.body:
The Vault of Doors is cold again, and Professor Permancer is walking round it with a bookmark held out in front of him like a divining rod.

Every ribbon in the room is pointing at somebody. They hang from the bookmark in a bunch, claret and green and one very faded blue, and each of them has found its person without being told: a ribbon for Wicker, who's standing with his hands behind his back and his chin up, as if posing for a portrait of himself being innocent. A ribbon for a first-year who's gone pink. A ribbon, a long and slightly smug one, for Penny.

“Names,” says Permancer. “Not heads. If you count heads you'll lose somebody who's been replaced.”

Penny checks the list. She doesn't glance at the total. That's the whole trick of her, and I've watched it for weeks: she never looks at the sum. She matches each name to its ribbon, one at a time, with the point of a pencil, saying them under her breath like a rosary, and only when every ribbon has answered does she let herself look down at the end of the page.

“Complete,” she says.

“Again,” says Permancer.

The ribbons have already started. They've let go of their people and swung back into the bunch, and they're beginning, one by one, to point again. It takes a long time. It's the most boring lesson in the Academy. Everybody in the room is quietly very pleased with it.

Wicker catches my eye, from across the Vault, and says without sound: *it's a lot of ribbon.* I'd like to say I didn't enjoy that.
beats.report: Permancer's class practiced matching each returning ribbon to a named traveller, not merely counting them.

beats.title: Ink Has No Conscience
beats.body:
Professor Villanelle has put Wicker's sentence on the board.

She's done it in her own chalk, in her own plain hand, with nothing added and nothing taken away. *For one sentence, let him choose the verb.* It sits at the front of the Inkworks like a specimen in a jar. The plaster behind it is very, very quiet.

Nobody laughs. It's the thing I notice first. Usually somebody laughs at a thing like that: the shape of the clause, the cheek of the word *let.* It's a good sentence, technically. It's neat. It has a lovely rhythm. It's the sort of sentence that could be quoted on a plaque.

Wicker's in the back row, with his hands under his knees, looking at it as though somebody else had written it.

“Read the verb,” says Villanelle.

There's a silence.

“There isn't one,” says Penny. “That's the point. He left it empty.”

“Yes.” Villanelle taps the gap with the chalk. It's a small clean tap, like a knock on a door. “A verb's the part of the sentence that does the thing. He gave it to someone else to fill.” She turns to the class. “Now tell me who had to live with it.”

Nobody answers. Wicker's ears have gone slowly, steadily red.

Villanelle doesn't press. She never presses. She stands with the chalk in her hand, looking at the board, and lets the question go on being asked until the whole room can feel it, in its feet, in its paper, in the bones of the desks.

“Ink has no conscience,” she says at last, quietly. “It goes where it's sent. The conscience is yours. Put it in the sentence *before* you write it. After, you're only a witness.”
beats.report: Villanelle's class studied the sentence Wicker wrote in the source and asked who bore its consequence.

beats.title: A Letter from Permancer
beats.body:
Reader—

I went back to the Vault before breakfast.

I put the list where Penny held it, and I stood where I'd stood on the Sunday. Every ribbon pointed home. The bookmark was warm and quiet in my hand. By any measure I've ever used, the lesson was a success.

Then I walked round it.

It's a simple thing to do, and I'd never done it in eleven years. I walked all the way round the open source, to the side I'd never stood on, and I looked at the doorway from the back. From the back it looked like a door.

The list told me everyone had come home. It hadn't counted who else crossed. I should have checked both sides before I invited anyone through. I should have asked who was standing on the other side of the page, and what they wanted, and whether anyone had asked *them.*

The new procedure's on my desk. It's eight lines long. There's a blank line at the bottom, for what I've still failed to ask.

If you bring back a look from the other side of something, I'd like to read it. Penny's making room beside the chalk outline.

—Permancer
beats.report: Permancer wrote to the Reader about the return list's blind side and the procedure he was changing.

beats.title: The Chair's Direction
beats.body:
Professor Wispwood has brought a chair into the Spark Annex, and she's turned it to face the class.

It's an ordinary chair. It's got four legs and a woven seat and a back with a small chip out of the left rail. It sits on the flagstones in the afternoon light with an expression of enormous patience, the way chairs do when they've been looked at.

“What's it saying?” she asks.

Nobody knows.

She turns it, with both hands, so that it faces the wall. She does it quite gently. Then she steps back, and clasps her hands behind her, and waits. It's amazing how different a chair is from behind. The back of it's all rungs and shadow. The seat, which was an offer, has become a shrug.

“Same chair,” she says. “Which way would you sit?”

A boy at the front says, “The first way.” A girl in the second row says, after a long pause, “I wouldn't sit in either.” Wispwood nods at both as if they'd given her tea.

Then the chair turns itself back.

It does it without a sound, a quarter-turn at a time, with a small apologetic scrape. It faces the class again. It's quite clear it's done that on purpose, and it's equally clear it's rather pleased.

“Thank you,” Wispwood tells it.

Somewhere near the back, Penny writes *invitation = direction + room* on a card, and underlines *room* twice.
beats.report: Wispwood's class tested how the direction of an ordinary chair could change an invitation.

beats.title: Rest After the Door
beats.body:
Professor Stonebrook takes the chalk out of the clock's hands.

I don't know how else to say it. The clock in the Still Room has had a bit of chalk since the Sunday, held in the crook of its minute-hand, and it's been writing the next thing on the wall at the end of every hour, as it's done for a hundred years. *Lesson. Lesson. Supper. Lesson.* He reaches up, takes the stub gently out of its grip, and puts it in his pocket.

For a little while, the room stops writing the next thing.

It's the most remarkable silence. Nothing's coming. The walls are bare. There's a window with a long wet light in it, and two chairs, one on each side, with a low table between them and a pot of tea nobody's poured.

There's a chair by the window. He sits in the other one.

That's the whole class. The students come in, one by one, in their coats, with their notebooks held in front of them like shields, and they look at the bare walls, and at the two chairs, and at the professor, who's sitting with his hands on his knees looking out at the rain. After a minute somebody sits down. After another minute, somebody else does.

Nobody asks what they're supposed to be learning.

“It's all right,” Stonebrook says eventually, to nobody, to the rain. “The door's closed. You can put your feet down.”
beats.report: Stonebrook made room for rest after the return rather than assigning another crossing.

beats.title: A Letter from Wicker
beats.body:
I repaired Serenity's map case.

The clasp was always crooked. I used to tell her so. She used to tell me to carry my own map.

So I straightened it. I did it very carefully, at two in the morning, with a file and a lot of brass I borrowed from the Vault. It looked wonderful. I was extremely proud of it. Then I tried closing it with one hand, the way she does, and I couldn't make it work, and I stood there at the workbench with the thing in my fingers, understanding something I'd been told in several different ways for several different months.

I put it back the way it was. The crooked way. It closes perfectly now, if you do it her way.

She's using it. She hasn't spoken to me about it.

I keep writing another sentence here. I've crossed it out so often the paper's gone soft.

Leave that bit alone.

—Wicker
beats.report: Wicker wrote that he repaired Serenity's map case and left the crooked clasp as she used it.

beats.title: Amendment in the Vault
beats.body:
Permancer's notice on the Vault door has a new line.

*An invitation can be held open, lit, arranged, or left waiting.*

It's written in his small upright hand, in fresh black ink, a little above where the old list ended. Below it, in somebody else's writing, square and economical and slightly slanted, there's an answer.

*Check what it means from the other side.*

That's Penny. She's put a small tick beside it, and a question mark beside the tick, as if she'd marked her own answer and found it didn't quite satisfy her.

The notice hangs a little way off the wall, on two brass pins, so you can lift it and read the back. Someone has already done it. There's a thumbprint on the lower corner, and on the reverse, in pencil, one word in a third hand: *Yes.*
beats.report: The Vault posted an amended invitation rule and Penny's instruction to check it from the other side.

beats.title: Receipt or Rumor
beats.body:
People say the red chair still appears after the East Stacks close.

It isn't in the East Stacks any more. It turns up in the corridor outside the Kitchens, or at the foot of the north stair, or in the middle of an otherwise empty classroom, a plain red chair with a worn seat and a good straight back. Nobody's seen it come. Nobody's seen it go.

It's facing the right way now.

Nobody can agree which way that is. A third-year says it faces the door. Ambrose says it faces the fire. Penny says that she's checked, from both sides, and that it depends where you're standing, which is what she'd say about most things.

I've been past it twice. I wanted it to face me. I'd like to say that it did.
beats.report: People disagreed about which way the red chair faced after the East Stacks closed.

entries.title: Lunch
entries.account: October began in the Kitchens. Ambrose Trencher pulled one chair out beside Serenity Brown's map, "in case." Wicker Eddies took the seat across from her and passed her the bigger half of the loaf. A supervised Jump into *Dracula* was already on the calendar for Sunday.

castMemories.aside: Chair's still out by her map. In case.

castMemories.memory: At lunch on the first day of October, Wicker passed Serenity the bigger half of the loaf.

entries.title: The long way
entries.account: Soren Ng left Serenity a folded paper bird with her map-boat drawn on its belly. One wing read *if you want the long way.* He waited for her three steps up the stair, a stub of chalk in each hand.

castMemories.memory: Soren left Serenity a folded paper bird with her boat on its belly, and waited three steps up the stair with chalk in each hand.
castMemories.aside: She found the bird. I'd folded four before that one. The other three were worse at waiting.

entries.title: The lesson
entries.account: On Sunday Professor Permancer took the Book Jump Club into *Dracula*. In the source margin, Wicker Eddies wrote: *For one sentence, let him choose the verb.* The Jump ended early. Permancer brought every registered Jumper home, and Penny Blackletter read the roll twice.

castMemories.memory: In the source margin of Dracula, Wicker wrote one sentence: for one sentence, let him choose the verb.
castMemories.aside: I gave him one verb. One. I keep doing the sum and it keeps coming out wrong.

castMemories.memory: Permancer brought every registered Jumper home from Dracula when the visit ended early.
castMemories.aside: Every name answered when Penny read the roll. I've never been so glad to feel four ribbons twitch.

castMemories.memory: Penny read the Jump roster twice after the class came home from Dracula. Every name answered.
castMemories.aside: Complete. I said it out loud, so it was true. I checked it again after supper anyway.

entries.title: Follow
entries.account: Dracula chose *follow*. He saw the reciprocal doorway and crossed under Permancer's invitation. The bookmark counted every registered Jumper home. It had never been asked to count anyone else.

castMemories.memory: The Count crossed into the Academy under Permancer's return invitation. The bookmark had never been asked to count anyone else.
castMemories.aside: All of you. I wrote it for my students. He read it as an invitation. He wasn't wrong, which is the worst part.

entries.title: The living claim
entries.account: Outside his source, Dracula began to lose his hold on the Academy. He deliberately harmed Serenity Brown and used the wound as a living claim. Serenity survived. Closed books began to sound like doors to her.

castMemories.memory: Dracula deliberately harmed Serenity and used her as a living claim to stay in the Academy. She survived, and closed books began to sound like doors to her.
castMemories.aside: Closed books sound like doors now. Knocking, mostly. I'm told that's not normal. I'm told a lot of things.

entries.title: Six harbours
entries.account: Soren Ng brought tracing paper to the Kitchens: Serenity's boat drawn into six harbours, the last one in the crook of an oak. She took his pencil and told him the tree would need a ladder. That week she built a tower from toast crusts and named it Permancer. It leaned.

castMemories.memory: Soren brought Serenity tracing paper with her boat drawn into six harbours, the last one in the crook of an oak.
castMemories.aside: Six harbours. She said the tree needs a ladder. She's right. I'm drawing a taller one.

castMemories.memory: Serenity built a tower of toast crusts in the Kitchens and named it Permancer. It leaned.
castMemories.aside: He's not falling over. He's leaning. It's different.

entries.title: A finished man
entries.account: The Academy found the Count reading his own ending. He wanted a tomorrow. He intended to keep the one he had taken.

entries.title: Through several books
entries.account: The Count left the Old Reading Room through several books. The black line on Serenity's map split into branches.

castMemories.memory: The Count left the Old Reading Room through several books, and the black line on Serenity's map split into branches.
castMemories.aside: The line on my map's gone everywhere. More ways than yesterday. Still true.

entries.title: Borrowed rooms
entries.account: His absence pulled neighboring stories into the East Stacks. A castle grew out of borrowed rooms. The Academy learned how to return him: an open source, a recognizable invitation, and Serenity's withdrawal of the claim.

castMemories.memory: The Academy learned that only Serenity could send the Count back, by withdrawing the living claim herself.
castMemories.aside: Only I can let go of it. Everyone says it gently, like I might drop it. I won't.

entries.title: Company
entries.account: A drawbridge grew across the Quillquarium, a window from another book's nursery appeared in a corridor, and a stair opened between the supper tables, going up to a hall nobody was invited to. All of it was closed to visitors. The Academy asked that nobody take the window home, or follow the soup.

entries.title: The return
entries.account: Ambrose brought terms. Permancer and Penny reconstructed the rule. Wicker made the paper threshold. Serenity pulled the black line free of her map. Dracula went back. The rooms followed.

castMemories.memory: Serenity pulled the black line free of her map and withdrew the living claim herself. Dracula went back to his source.
castMemories.aside: What he changed in me is mine now. I said that out loud, in front of everybody. I meant every word.

castMemories.memory: Ambrose brought the terms that sent the Count back to his source.
castMemories.aside: Brought terms. Same as supper. You put the paper down where everyone can see it.

castMemories.memory: Wicker made the paper threshold the Count went back through.
castMemories.aside: I folded a door out of old menus. It worked. Nobody's more surprised than me.

castMemories.memory: Penny and Permancer worked out the rule for the return: source, invitation, and a claim only Serenity could release.
castMemories.aside: We worked out the rule on cards. It held. I've kept the cards in case it needs to hold again.

castMemories.memory: Permancer and Penny reconstructed the rule that sent the Count back to his source.
castMemories.aside: Penny did the hard part. I did the part where you stand still and hold a book open. I'm good at that part.

entries.title: Nightbound
entries.account: Serenity still heard the page-turns. At breakfast she chose the name Nightbound. Permancer pinned a new return list by the Vault: every traveller named, the doorway checked from both sides. Ordinary teaching Jumps were suspended while the safeguards were fitted.

castMemories.memory: Serenity still heard the page-turns, and at breakfast she chose the name for it: Nightbound.
castMemories.aside: Nightbound. It's my word. Penny wrote it on a card, but she waited until I nodded.

castMemories.memory: Permancer pinned a new return list by the Vault, and ordinary teaching Jumps were suspended while the safeguards were fitted.
castMemories.aside: No Jumps until it's right. The students are furious. Good. They should want it that much.

entries.title: Not today
entries.account: Wicker asked to enter the Kitchens. Serenity told him, “Not today.” She added a rule to the new list: anyone who maps what she hears has to ask her first. The next day's lessons began with the notice still drying.

castMemories.memory: Wicker asked Serenity if he could come into the Kitchens. She said not today.
castMemories.aside: She said not today. I said all right. Easiest thing I've said all month, and the hardest.

entries.title: Threshold Protocols
entries.account:
The Academy opened a door. Someone came the other way.

Permancer has written these beside the Vault:

1. Name the source and why you are entering it.
2. Name every traveller allowed to return.
3. Close the invitation around those names.
4. Check the doorway from both sides.
5. Leave the people in the source their own lives. No experiments on them for the sake of a lesson.
6. No living anchors.
7. Ask before using what a changed person can do.
8. After the return, check what came back different.

Penny has pinned the old list beside the new one. The old one is complete. That's why she kept it.

castMemories.memory: Permancer wrote eight Threshold Protocols beside the Vault. The last says to check what came back different.
castMemories.aside: Eight rules now. The old list was perfectly good. It just never asked what to do when someone wants to come back with you.

castMemories.memory: Penny pinned Permancer's old Jump list beside the new one, because it was complete.
castMemories.aside: I kept the old list up. It's not wrong. It's just short. Things can be both.

entries.title: The clasp
entries.account: Wicker Eddies mended Serenity's map case and put the new clasp on crooked, because she fastens it with one hand. Soren Ng's folded bird stayed with her. In the Book Burrow she said she liked a question Soren had asked, and that she still wanted to ask Wicker what he'd meant to happen.

castMemories.memory: Wicker mended Serenity's map case and set the new clasp a little crooked, because she fastens it with one hand.
castMemories.aside: I mended a map case. It took all night. Nobody's said thank you, which is fine, because nobody's supposed to know.

castMemories.aside: She kept the bird. She liked my question. I've been trying not to ask another one too quickly.

catchUp.title: A School With a Dangerous Library
catchUp.body:
It's October, and the Academy is being an ordinary school. That's its most suspicious mood.

Lunch happens in the Kitchens. Ambrose Trencher stirs a pot you could bathe a professor in, and every day he pulls one chair out from the table "in case." Next to that chair sits Serenity Brown, with a map she can't stop adding to. Her boat is the size of a lentil. Across from her, Wicker Eddies sits down like he's arriving on a stage, and hands her the bigger half of the bread without looking at it.

On Sunday, Professor Permancer takes the Book Jump Club into *Dracula*. It's on the calendar. Nobody's worried. That's what worries me.

catchUp.title: The Jump Ended Early
catchUp.body:
Sunday's Jump into *Dracula* ended early. Wicker Eddies wrote one sentence in the source margin that nobody had allowed: *For one sentence, let him choose the verb.* Professor Permancer opened the return, every registered traveller answered the bookmark, and Penny read the roll twice. The source is shut while the sentence is examined. Afterwards a word was found missing from my stitching. I'm taking that personally.

Asked if it was a prank, Wicker said, "I meant it." He didn't say what he'd meant. He was sitting on the Vault floor with ink on his knee, and he didn't look like a boy who was enjoying himself.

Everything else is as it was. Ambrose still pulls out the chair beside Serenity's map, in case.

catchUp.title: The East Stacks Are Shut
catchUp.body:
Dracula didn't stay in his book. He crossed out during Sunday's return, and on Thursday he used Serenity Brown to hold himself inside the Academy. Ambrose carried her from the East Stacks to the Kitchens. Wicker brought water and held the door.

The East Stacks are closed to everyone, including the books. Serenity's awake, and she can hear page-turns from books that are shut, like somebody in the next room reading slowly. She's deciding what help she wants to give. The deciding is hers. Visits go through Ambrose, who has put a ladle on the door. Her map has started to trace where the Count goes.

Permancer admits he opened the return invitation. Wicker admits he changed the source. Both are helping, and both have been asked to stop saying *technically.* Before all this, Soren Ng left Serenity a folded bird with her boat drawn on its belly. One wing said *if you want the long way.*
catchUp.openQuestion: What is the line on her map following?

catchUp.title: Six Harbours
catchUp.body:
The East Stacks are shut, the Count is loose, and Serenity's awake in the Kitchens, deciding one day at a time who gets to see her. She can hear page-turns from shut books. Her map keeps tracing where the Count goes, whether she touches it or not.

A few days after she was up, Soren came in carrying tracing paper the way you'd carry a sleeping animal. He'd drawn her boat into six harbours: a teacup, a lighthouse lamp, under a bridge, inside a bell, a drowned cathedral font, and the crook of a very big oak. She took his pencil and said the tree would need a ladder. That week she built a tower out of toast crusts and named it Permancer. It leans.

catchUp.title: He Got Away
catchUp.body:
They found the Count in the Old Reading Room. He was reading his own book, with a pencil, and he'd reached the ending. He's a finished man, and he wants a tomorrow. He means to keep the one he took.

Serenity went in to speak to him. She came out again and went directly to lunch. Nobody's asked her what he said. Afterwards the Count left through several books, one after another, and the black line on her map split into branches.

Professor Villanelle put Wicker's sentence on the board, and nobody laughed. Permancer has been in the Vault since before breakfast. Penny went round the back of the chalk door to see what's there, and it has a back. Permancer followed. They both came out again, and neither of them will say what they saw.

catchUp.title: The Academy Has Company
catchUp.body:
With the Count loose, his neighbours have been moving in. A castle made of borrowed rooms has grown through the East Stacks: a library at the bottom, a fortress in the middle, a nursery at the top. A polite drawbridge now crosses the Quillquarium, and it's closed to visitors. A window from some other book's nursery has turned up in a corridor. Please don't take it home. A stair has opened between the supper tables, going up to a hall nobody was invited to. The soup is warm up there. Don't follow the soup.

The Academy has worked out how to send everything home. It takes three things: the source, an invitation the Count will recognise, and Serenity's withdrawal of the living claim. The first two can be built. The third can't be built by anyone but the person who holds it. Serenity put her hand over that card. She's agreed to the return, and the last condition is hers to release.

catchUp.title: The Night He Went Home
catchUp.body:
He's gone home. Ambrose brought the terms, Permancer opened the book, Penny checked the threshold, and Wicker held the fold. Serenity withdrew the living claim herself, and the borrowed rooms fell back into words: the castle, the drawbridge, the nursery window, the stair. I lost a stitch holding the source open.

Serenity can still hear the page-turns. At breakfast she chose a word for what she hears: *Nightbound.* Permancer pinned a new return list by the Vault. Every traveller has to be named, and the doorway gets checked from both sides. Ordinary teaching Jumps are suspended while the safeguards are fitted.
catchUp.openQuestion: What does Nightbound mean for her?

catchUp.title: Not Today
catchUp.body:
He's gone home. Ambrose brought the terms, Permancer opened the book, Penny checked the threshold, and Wicker held the fold. Serenity withdrew the living claim herself, and the borrowed rooms fell back into words. I lost a stitch holding the source open.

Serenity can still hear the page-turns. At breakfast she chose a word for what she hears: *Nightbound.* Permancer pinned a new return list by the Vault, and she added a rule of her own: anyone who maps what she hears has to ask her first.

Then Wicker asked if he could come into the Kitchens. Serenity said, "Not today."
catchUp.openQuestion: What will she do with "not today"?

catchUp.title: What's on the Table
catchUp.body:
October's over, and it hasn't shut all its doors. Lessons are back. The Quillquarium splashes downward again.

Wicker mended Serenity's map case. He put the new clasp on crooked, and it closes perfectly, because he'd noticed she fastens it with one hand. Soren's folded bird is still with her, and this week he asked her a whole question about the glass roof, with a question mark on the end. She said she liked that. She also said she still wants to ask Wicker what he meant to happen, once she can bear to listen.

The bird and the map case are on a table in the Book Burrow, in the same lamplight.

storyScenes.title: The chair that gets there first
storyScenes.opening:
It's lunchtime, and you're carrying me, which means I get to smell everything first.

I haven't got a nose. I've got paper, and paper remembers every kitchen it's ever been near. So when we pass the third door on the left, my back cover goes warm and starts to smell of onions and bay and burnt toast, and I lean in your arm the only way I can. You notice the lean. You always do. We go in.

The Kitchens are the most honest room in the Academy. Everywhere else, the Labyrinth pretends to be a school. In here it admits it's a place where people get hungry. The ceiling's black from three hundred years of steam. The tables are long and scrubbed pale, and every inch of them has been carved by someone who was told not to. There's a fire in a hearth big enough to hold a lecture, and in front of it Ambrose Trencher stands behind a pot you could bathe a professor in.

He's fishing something out of it with a ladle.

“Bay leaf,” he says, in the voice of a man being very reasonable.

The thing on the ladle has legs. It has a great many, and all of them are moving.

“Ambrose.”

“It's a bay leaf that's had an idea.” He lowers the ladle to the windowsill and waits. “It can leave under its own steam.”

It does. It goes over the sill and into the rain at a speed that says it's been planning this since the garden.

Halfway down the nearest table, Serenity Brown has built a country. Her map is spread between the salt and a heel of bread, and she's weighed its corners down with whatever came to hand: a spoon, a teacup, an egg in an eggcup with a paper flag stuck in the top. There are mountains in pencil. There's a river she inked in blue that's dried darker than she meant. There's a small sea, too, because she knocked over her water and decided that was where the sea had always been.

She's drawing a boat on it. The boat is the size of a lentil. It's got a flag.

“Weather,” she says to the map, and moves her bowl uphill.

Ambrose has pulled one chair out from the table, the one right beside her map. He does it every lunch, before anybody's sat down. If you ask him why, he says, “In case.” If you ask him in case of what, he says, “Soup.”

Across the table, a second chair scrapes.

Wicker Eddies has hold of it. He pulls out a chair the way other people open a door in a play, with a pause at the end for the audience. His collar's turned up against a draught I can tell you isn't there.

“That seat's taken,” Serenity says, without looking up.

“By whom?”

“Someone I haven't met yet.”

“Excellent.” He sits. “They'll be late. People you haven't met always are.”

She gives him a look. It's a short one, the kind you give a cat that's walked across your homework. Then she draws a bog on his half of the map.

Wicker steals her pencil. He's very quick about it. He draws stepping stones across the bog, one after another, each a little too far from the next to be any use. It takes him almost no time, and he doesn't look at her while he does it. That's how you know he's pleased.

Serenity studies the stones. Then she takes the pencil back and draws a very small Wicker in the water. He's up to his knees. He's got his collar up.

Wicker leans closer, and for a moment the two of them are bent over the same inch of paper.

“My hair's better than that.”

“It's wet.”

“It's *swimming*.”

“Then it's got the right idea.”

Ambrose puts a bowl down between them, exactly in the middle, with a heel of bread beside it. Both of them reach. Both of them get a hand on it. Neither of them lets go.

I'm in the crook of your arm, and I can feel you deciding where to sit.

nodes.body:
Wicker wins the bread, or lets her think he doesn't. He tears the loaf and hands Serenity the bigger half without looking at it, the way you'd hand someone a coat.

She notices. Of course she notices. She looks at the piece in her hand, then at the smaller one in his, and without a word she breaks a corner off hers and sets it down in the middle of his bog.

“Land,” she says. “Try to stay on it.”

Wicker looks at the crumb for a good while. Then he looks at the stepping stones he drew, each one too far from the next, and he moves one of them closer. It's a very small distance. It's about the width of a crumb.

Nobody says anything. Ambrose, passing with the ladle, says something with his eyebrows.

By now I've got a few crumbs of my own. They fall between my pages whenever you lean over the table, and they're the best thing anyone's given me all week. Ambrose says he'll shake me out later. He says that every time. He never has.

storyScenes.title: A sentence with its coat off
storyScenes.opening:
The Inkworks smells of wet slate and pencil shavings, and it's the only classroom in the Academy where the walls are listening on purpose.

You can tell by the plaster. It bulges a little, here and there, like a throat about to say something. Professor Villanelle ignores it. She's standing at the board with a stub of chalk and the expression of a woman who's about to commit a small, necessary murder.

She's written a sentence.

*The ineffable splendour of dawn bestowed a profound sense of possibility upon the weary traveller.*

Somewhere behind the plaster, something coughs.

It's a modest cough. It's the cough of a sentence that's been wearing a great many words for a great many years and has just noticed the draught.

Villanelle lets us all finish reading. She doesn't hurry people with a sentence. Then she turns, and the chalk goes behind her back like a conjuror's coin.

“What happened?”

Penny Blackletter's hand goes up before the question's finished. She's got ink on her cuff and a catalogue card in her teeth, and she takes the card out to answer.

“Someone got up.”

“Where?”

“The sentence hasn't said.”

“What did they see?”

Penny looks at the board again. She's thorough. She reads it the way other people check a lock. “It hasn't said that either.”

“No,” says Villanelle, almost fondly. “It hasn't.”

She rubs out *ineffable*. The chalk squeals. It's a thin, high sound, and the plaster behind the board winces. She doesn't stop. She rubs out *splendour*, and *bestowed*, and *profound*, one after another, until what's left on the board is a skeleton with a wristwatch.

“I was at the bus stop,” she says. “It was a Tuesday. I had a headache that made the light feel personal. And somebody had left an orange on the bench.”

She wipes out what's left, and writes again, in plainer chalk:

*There was an orange on the wet bench, bright enough that I nearly missed the bus.*

The thing in the wall stops coughing. It lets out a long breath, and for a second the whole room smells, very faintly, of orange peel.

I like the orange. I like it a great deal. I'm a book; I live in sentences, and most of them are standing about in their best coats. This one's standing in the rain with its collar open and it's the only one in the room I'd follow home.

“That's all I'm asking,” says Villanelle. “Find the thing that was actually there. Then say it, and stop.”

Across the room, Serenity has been writing something of her own. She's got her arm curled round the page, the way you do when you don't want the page to be seen. Wicker, two desks over, has become interested in the ceiling. Then in the window. Then, by a wide and unconvincing arc, in Serenity.

He leans sideways to read.

She puts her hand flat over the page.

“Ask.”

“Is it about me?”

“It was about something that needed throwing out.” She slides the paper under her elbow. “I can see why you'd be hopeful.”

“I'm not hopeful. I'm professionally curious.”

“You're sitting on my sleeve.”

He is. He moves, not very far.

Villanelle reaches between them. She doesn't say a word. She just takes a fresh sheet of paper off Wicker's desk and sets it in front of him, squarely, like a plate.

“Your turn.”

He looks at it. It looks back. It's blank, and a little smug about it. He's a boy who has an answer ready for every insult in the Labyrinth, and the blank page has never been insulted in its life.

For once in his life, it gets the first word.

At the front of the room Villanelle looks, briefly, at you. She doesn't say anything. She taps the board where the orange is, twice, with the end of the chalk, the way you'd tap a door you hope someone will open later.

*Not today,* the tap says. *But you'll have a true one somewhere. Keep an eye out.*
storyScenes.braidText: Villanelle rubbed the grand words off the board. Underneath was an orange on a wet bus-stop bench. I could get my teeth round that.

castMemories.memory: Villanelle rubbed the grand words off a sentence on the Inkworks board and wrote an orange on a wet bus-stop bench in their place.
castMemories.aside: I still think about that orange. It was a real one. I didn't eat it. I nearly missed the bus.

castMemories.memory: Penny answered first in Villanelle's lesson: someone got up, and the sentence hadn't said where.
castMemories.aside: That sentence never said where they got up. I've checked it four more times since. It still doesn't.

castMemories.memory: Serenity covered her page with her hand when Wicker leaned over to read it, and told him it was about something that needed throwing out.
castMemories.aside: Wicker asked if my page was about him. It wasn't. It's not my fault he looked so hopeful.

castMemories.memory: Villanelle set a blank sheet in front of Wicker, and for once he had nothing to say to it.
castMemories.aside: A blank page beat me in an argument. It didn't even say anything. That's the trick, apparently.

storyScenes.title: The wrong way to the classroom
storyScenes.opening:
Serenity has lost the classroom.

She knows exactly where it was. She drew a very good map of it yesterday, with a compass-rose and a small boat. But the North Staircase has taken the map personally, and the corridor outside the Map Room has turned itself, quietly, a quarter-turn to the left.

“We could ask someone,” I say. Serenity's used to me by now. She doesn't even jump.

“We're almost there.”

We've passed the same boot three times. It's a very good boot, a brown one, laced to the top and abandoned in the exact middle of the floor, and by the third pass it's begun to look confident.

Serenity doesn't stop walking. She walks the way she does everything: slightly sideways, as if there's a better thing beyond the thing in front of her and she's already half seen it.

On the next windowsill, there's a paper bird.

It's folded from good paper, cream-coloured and thick, with a crisp little tail and two wings held out like a person weighing a decision. There's writing on both wings. Under the left, in small blue letters: *if you want the room.* Under the right: *if you want the long way.*

Serenity picks it up. She turns it over. There's a drawing on its belly, in pencil, so small you'd miss it if you weren't a book. It's her boat. It's got the flag.

“Soren,” she says.

She sounds pleased, and then, almost at once, a little cross about sounding pleased. She frowns at the two wings.

“He could have waited for us.”

“He didn't want to,” I say. “He wanted you to find it.”

“That's not the same thing.”

“No,” I say. “It's better.”

She doesn't answer that. She takes the left-hand door.

Soren Ng is sitting on the stair beyond it, three steps up, with a stub of chalk in each hand and an expression that was clearly meant to look accidental. He's got ink-blue cuffs and a patient face. He's the sort of boy who arranges your surprise, steps back, and then pretends to be looking at the ceiling.

“The long way has a glass roof,” he says, as if she'd asked.

“You put my boat on a bird.”

“It needed to get upstairs.”

“It was *my* boat.”

“It's a very good boat.” He says it plainly, without a joke on it. It lands on her in a way I can see. Noticing that kind of thing is most of what I'm for.

She sits down beside him to look at the fold. He shows her where the paper turns, a crease so slight you'd think the bird had done it itself, and how the whole wing's held up by a single pinch near the shoulder. Their hands meet there. His waits, and she finishes the fold.

Neither of them says anything about that either. It's turning into a very quiet staircase.

Then Wicker Eddies comes through the classroom door behind them.

It's the classroom. It's right there. It was always right there, at the top of the *other* stair, and he's strolling out of it with his hands in his pockets and a look of mild amusement that has clearly been waiting for an audience.

“How elaborate,” he says. He looks at the bird, at the chalk, at the pair of them sitting close together on a step. “Have you tried saying hello?”

“Hello, Wicker,” Soren says.

He says it kindly, and that's what gets under Wicker's collar. You can see it go in.

Serenity laughs into the bird.

Serenity picks it up. She turns it over. There's a drawing on its belly, in pencil, so small you'd miss it if you weren't a book. It's her boat. It's got the flag.

“Soren,” she says.

She sounds pleased, and then, almost at once, a little cross about sounding pleased. She frowns at the two wings.

“He could have waited for us.”

“He didn't want to,” I say. “He wanted you to find it.”

“That's not the same thing.”

“No,” I say. “It's better.”

She doesn't answer that. She takes the left-hand door.

Soren Ng is sitting on the stair beyond it, three steps up, with a stub of chalk in each hand and an expression that was clearly meant to look accidental. He's got ink-blue cuffs and a patient face. He's the sort of boy who arranges your surprise, steps back, and then pretends to be looking at the ceiling.

“The long way has a glass roof,” he says, as if she'd asked.

“You put my boat on a bird.”

“It needed to get upstairs.”

“It was *my* boat.”

“It's a very good boat.” He says it plainly, without a joke on it. It lands on her in a way I can see. Noticing that kind of thing is most of what I'm for.

She sits down beside him to look at the fold. He shows her where the paper turns, a crease so slight you'd think the bird had done it itself, and how the whole wing's held up by a single pinch near the shoulder. Their hands meet there. His waits, and she finishes the fold.

Neither of them says anything about that either. It's turning into a very quiet staircase.

Then Wicker Eddies comes through the classroom door behind them.

It's the classroom. It's right there. It was always right there, at the top of the *other* stair, and he's strolling out of it with his hands in his pockets and a look of mild amusement that has clearly been waiting for an audience.

“How elaborate,” he says. He looks at the bird, at the chalk, at the pair of them sitting close together on a step. “Have you tried saying hello?”

“Hello, Wicker,” Soren says.

He says it kindly, and that's what gets under Wicker's collar. You can see it go in.

Serenity laughs into the bird.

choices.title: “Show us the glass roof.”
choices.result:
“Show us the glass roof.”

Soren stands up too quickly. He drops a chalk stub, and it rolls, and he has to retrieve it from under Serenity's shoe. She lifts her foot very slowly, and he goes very red, and nobody says a word about it.

Wicker, in the doorway, says several, privately, to himself.
choices.braidText: You asked Soren to show you the glass roof. He dropped his chalk getting up.

castMemories.memory: The reader asked Soren to show them the glass roof. He stood up too fast and dropped his chalk under Serenity's shoe.
castMemories.aside: You asked about the glass roof. I dropped my chalk. I'd planned the roof part. I hadn't planned the chalk part.

choices.title: “Serenity can choose.”
choices.result:
“Serenity can choose.”

She looks at the classroom door, then at the bird, then back at the door, as if it's a dish she's already eaten. “Roof,” she says. “We already know what a room looks like.”

Soren stands as if he's been given something. Wicker pretends it's about the ceiling.
choices.braidText: You left the choice to Serenity. She chose the roof.

castMemories.memory: The reader left the choice to Serenity, and she chose the roof over the room.
castMemories.aside: You let me choose. People don't, much. I chose the roof. We already knew what a room looked like.

choices.title: “Class first. Roof after.”
choices.result:
“Class first. Roof after.”

“Someone write that down,” Wicker says. “A plan with an *after*.” But he holds the classroom door open for them, and he stays holding it while they collect the chalk, and he doesn't make a single remark about the bird. That's how you know he's thinking about it.
choices.braidText: You suggested class first and the roof afterwards. Wicker held the classroom door.

castMemories.memory: The reader said class first and the roof after, and Wicker held the classroom door for everyone and said nothing about the bird.
castMemories.aside: A plan with an after. I held the door for that. Somebody had to, and I had a hand free.

castMemories.memory: Soren left a folded paper bird with Serenity's boat drawn on its belly, and waited three steps up the North Staircase for her to find it.
castMemories.aside: She found the bird. I'd folded four before that one. The other three were worse at waiting.

castMemories.memory: Serenity found Soren's paper bird on a windowsill, with her own boat drawn on its belly, and finished its fold with him on the stair.
castMemories.aside: Soren put my boat on a bird. Without asking. It's a very good bird, which is annoying.

castMemories.memory: Wicker came out of the right classroom and found Serenity and Soren on the stair with a paper bird. Soren said hello to him, kindly.
castMemories.aside: Soren said hello to me. Nicely. I've been trying to work out what he meant by it ever since.

nodes.title: The wrong way to the classroom
nodes.body:
The glass roof can wait. It's good at that. It's been waiting for the right person since before any of us were bound.

In the bustle of picking up chalk, nobody's watching the windowsill, which is when I do it. I tip myself toward the paper bird, very slightly, and brush the tip of its tail with the end of my ribbon.

The bird nips my ribbon back.

It's a small, sharp, delighted nip, and I've never been so pleased in my life.

When we go in to the lesson, there's a drawing on the corner of Serenity's page that wasn't there this morning. It's a boat. It's got a flag. It's sitting at the foot of a very tall glass staircase, waiting to be asked.
nodes.braidText: I nipped the paper bird’s tail. It nipped my ribbon back.

storyScenes.title: Sunday Book Jump Club
storyScenes.opening:
The Vault of Doors is cold in a way that has nothing to do with weather. It's the cold of a place where a great many exits are being held shut by main force.

It's a round room, and everything in it that isn't a door is a lock. There are doors of oak and doors of glass; there's a door that's only a drawing of a door, and a door in the ceiling with a tiny ladder leading up to it that's been retired for reasons nobody mentions. Brass handles hang in rows along the walls like hooks in a cloakroom, polished by Sunday. Even the dangerous ones are keeping very still, the way a dog does when it's been told it might come along.

Professor Permancer is kneeling in the middle of the floor with a ribbon.

He's got his sleeves rolled and his tie tucked into his shirt, and he looks exactly like what he is: a man who's spent his whole career putting people into books and has, every single time, brought them back. He lays the ribbon straight across the flagstones.

“This end stays here,” he says.

The ribbon crawls toward his shoe.

“*Approximately* here.”

It stops. It sulks, in the way of silk.

Let me tell you what's about to happen, because nobody's going to say it plainly, and I think you ought to know.

Every book is a house. Most houses have a door nobody uses, and in a book it's the crease: the narrow seam down the middle where the two halves meet and the pages bend into the dark. If you know the way of it, and have the right sentence, and open the book at the right page and hold it open long enough, that seam isn't a seam. It's a threshold. You can step through into the story, and you'll find it exactly as the author left it, with the furniture in the right places and the weather already decided.

That's a Book Jump. It's the most dangerous lesson at the Academy, and Professor Permancer has taught it every Sunday for eleven years without losing a single student. This is why he's still allowed to teach it.

There are two rules, and he says them both before he lets anybody near the door.

“You don't touch what isn't yours. You don't accept anything you're offered.” He holds up two fingers. “The people in the book aren't props. They live there. We're guests, and guests behave.”

Then he shows us the ribbon.

It's a long, thin, ordinary ribbon, the colour of old claret, and one end of it's knotted into his bookmark. That's where it's anchored. That's the Vault's end, and it stays here, in this cold room, tied to the one thing in the building that's never been lost.

“A person walks through the crease,” he says, “and the ribbon pays out behind them. It doesn't snag. It doesn't tangle. It doesn't leave. When it's time to come home, you take hold of it and follow it back, hand over hand, and it leads you out the exact way you came in. You don't use any other way. You don't take shortcuts. Your ribbon *is* the way home.”

He makes a loop and passes the free end through it. Then he does it again, slowly, so we can all see his fingers.

Penny copies him on the first try, and then does it again to be sure. Wicker Eddies produces something that's technically a knot and has caught his thumb in it, and he stands there with his hand held up and an expression of immense dignity until Permancer reaches over and frees him without a word.

Now, something about *your* ribbon. It's tied to me.

I'm not being sentimental. It's a practical decision. The way home has to be fastened to something that won't be left behind, and a book that someone's carrying is the one object a traveller will never put down by accident. So Permancer takes the end of your ribbon, which is longer than the others and, I think, the best, and he threads it through my head-band and ties it off at my spine with a knot he checks twice.

I haven't got hands, if you've been wondering. I've got ribbons, and corners, and the great leaning power of my whole cover. I can't *hold* your way home. But I can *be* it, and I'm quite good at that, and I'll tell you if anything pulls.

“For this first visit,” I say, to you, “I'm keeping the line. You don't owe me a sentence to find your way home. Some day, if you've kept something real, a thing you really noticed, I can tie your ribbon to *that,* and it will hold better than silk. But not today. Today it's me.”

Permancer touches the ribbon where it crosses the floor. A little door opens in the air above the knot, no bigger than a window, and through it I can see his own office: the green lamp, the ink-stained blotter, and a cup of tea he's been looking for since breakfast. He reaches through, takes the cup, and brings his hand back with a small and satisfied sound.

“Now,” he says, to the room. “Where was my way home?”

Everyone points at the ribbon.

“Good. Keep looking at it,” he says, “whenever there's something more interesting to look at.”

*That* is the hardest part, and there's nobody in the room who knows it yet except him and me.

choices.title: Enter the supervised Jump
choices.result:
I've got your ribbon. Penny has the list. Permancer has the door.

Step up to the book, and don't let go of me.

choices.title: Stay in the Vault
choices.result: You stay in the Vault, in the cold, with the doors. That's allowed. It's a real part of the lesson, and Permancer says so. I'll keep your place on this side of the cover and tell you everything, afterwards, as truthfully as I can.

castMemories.memory: Professor Permancer taught the Book Jump Club the two rules and the ribbon, and tied the reader's ribbon to the Book itself.
castMemories.aside: Don't touch what isn't yours. Don't accept what you're offered. I've said it for eleven years. I say it slower now.

castMemories.memory: Wicker tied his practice knot round his own thumb, and Permancer freed him without a word.
castMemories.aside: My knot was technically a knot. It was technically attached to me. Permancer didn't need to look so tired about it.

nodes.title: Sunday Book Jump Club
nodes.body:
The class gathers by the lectern, where the book lies open under a single lamp.

It's an old copy, black-bound, with a cracked spine and a thumbprint of candle-grease on the title page. *Dracula*, by Bram Stoker. A hundred and thirty years of readers have worn the edges of it soft. It's very, very quiet. I don't like it. It's the quiet of a thing that's listening.

“Roster,” Penny murmurs, and takes out the list.

She's the one with the list. That's her whole job, and it's the most important one in the room. She checks it against a second list, and then a third, in a handwriting so small and even it looks printed.

“Permancer. Wicker. Me. You.”

“Still no Dracula?” Wicker asks.

“He lives there.”

“Then he can make the tea.”

“We don't accept food,” Permancer says, without looking up from his knots. “Or shelter, or conversation, or a chair. We enter by the front door and we walk the hall as far as the first landing. We look at the room. We come back. If you take nothing and ask for nothing and touch nothing, you'll have the most boring afternoon of your life.”

“That's what I'm hoping for,” says Penny, and writes it down.

I look for Serenity. She's by the Vault door, with her map folded under her arm and her chin up, the way she stands when she's decided to be easy about something she isn't easy about. She doesn't look at the book. She looks at Wicker, once, for a second longer than she means.

“I'll be in the East Stacks if anyone wants me,” she says. “Finishing the map. Bring me back something that isn't a bite.”

“It's a *lesson*,” says Wicker, wounded.

“It's a vampire,” says Serenity, and goes.

He watches the door she went through for much too long. Then he turns back and takes up his pen as if nothing's happened, which tells you everything.

Ribbons run from Permancer's bookmark to every name on Penny's list. Each is tied at the far end to the thing the traveller carries, a satchel strap, a button, a cuff. Yours runs to me, and I can feel the whole length of it, a thin cold line running back across the Vault and over the lip of the open book.

Don't pull. I'm holding something at the other end, and I'd like to go on holding it.

choices.title: The knot.
choices.result: You press a thumb to the knot at my spine. It tightens under your finger, with a small, warm, intelligent twitch, like a cat deciding to stay.
choices.braidText: Before entering Dracula, you checked the knot. It tightened beneath your finger.

choices.title: Your name on the list.
choices.result: You find your name on Penny's list. The ink is warm, as if it's only just been written. You check the other names too. All four are there, in a row, and for the first time you realise how few of them there are.
choices.braidText: Before entering Dracula, you checked your name and the other travellers on Penny's list.

castMemories.memory: Before the Jump, the reader checked their own name on Penny's list, and every other name too.
castMemories.aside: You checked the whole list. Most people only look for their own name. I notice everyone who checks.

choices.title: The way home.
choices.result: You look at the way home. From this side, the open book shows a doorway the colour of the Vault, the lamp, the lectern, the cold. If you lean sideways and look again, from the other side of the crease, you can see something else entirely: a long table, in the dark, waiting.
choices.braidText: Before entering Dracula, you checked the way home. The Vault waited on the other side.

castMemories.memory: Before stepping into Dracula, the reader looked back at the way home.
castMemories.aside: You looked at the way home before you went in. That's the whole lesson. You had it before I'd finished teaching it.

castMemories.memory: Penny read the roster for the Jump into Dracula: Permancer, Wicker, Penny, and the reader.
castMemories.aside: Four names on the roster. I read it twice going in. I'd read it a third time if anybody asked.

castMemories.memory: Serenity didn't go on the Jump. She went to finish her map in the East Stacks and told Wicker to bring her back something that wasn't a bite.

nodes.title: One verb
nodes.body:
Permancer steps into the book first.

He doesn't *go* anywhere. That's what you notice. One moment he's a man in a waistcoat with a bookmark in his hand, standing in front of a lectern, and the next the page has tilted a little, the way a table tilts when a child leans on it, and the man in the waistcoat has stopped being at the lectern and become, very gently, a thing that's already inside. Penny goes after him with her list held to her chest like a hymn-book.

Then the ribbon takes you by the hand. I'll say that once, and I'll mean it: it takes *you*, the whole of you, by every nerve. It draws you toward the seam.

*Now,* the book says. It says it without a voice, just a pressure at the back of every sense you have.

**It's like this.**

The crease opens, and the first thing it does is *smell*. It smells of cold brass, and of rain in a house with the windows shut, and underneath that of something sweet and old, a smell so far back in the paper that it must have been wine once, or blood, or ink. The Vault falls away and the smell closes round you like a coat.

Then the sound comes up through your feet. It's a long, low, rolling tone, the sound of a page being turned by something the size of a field, and under it you can hear the letters. They're all around you, the words themselves, whispering in their thousands, a dry, rising, rustling noise like a wind going through dead leaves. You can *taste* them. They taste like pencil and cold tea. They taste like the inside of a drawer.

You're falling, and not downward. You're falling *along*. You're falling the way a sentence goes: left to right, and then down to the next line, and then the next, every word a stair, and your shoes are catching on the *s*es and sliding on the *l*s. The words are racing underneath you in black ranks, thick as a crowd. Capital letters go by like tall men in hats. Commas curl away under your heels. A semicolon opens like a trapdoor and you hear yourself shout, soundlessly, in a colour you've never seen before, a greenish violet, the colour of a bruise on a leaf.

And somewhere behind it all, in the exact centre of the dark, there's a ribbon, thin and red and perfectly steady. It hums. It's the only straight thing in the world. It runs from your hand to my spine and it doesn't waver, not for a second, and so neither do you.

Stone catches your feet.

You land on a floor that's *damp*. That's the first and most surprising thing. It's a cold flagged floor, scoured by ten thousand years of a single winter, and in the half dark ahead of you there's a table.

It's the longest table you've ever seen. It runs into the gloom without troubling to end. A single orange sits at the far side of it, under a chandelier hung with a hundred unlit candles, and in all the black and silver and grey of that room the orange looks like a lamp somebody's forgotten to turn off.

I put out a corner to see it better. I can't help it. It's an *orange.* It's a perfectly ordinary orange, and it's the only thing in the book that's the colour of anything, and I lean toward it with my whole fore-edge like a plant toward a window.

A hand closes on my cover. It's Penny's.

“Observe,” she whispers.

“I *am* observing.”

“With your edges,” she says, very low. “Put them away.”

I put them away. It's the hardest thing I've done all day.

Then a door opens at the end of the hall, and Count Dracula comes in.

He's tall and he's dressed in black, and he's very nearly handsome, and he moves like water finding its level. He walks the whole of the long room without a sound, and he stops at the table, beside a high-backed chair, and puts one hand on it.

“You have come a long way,” he says, to nobody.

He doesn't see us. That's what Permancer meant by *held*. There's a paragraph, a particular one, a long black rectangle of Stoker's best prose, and he's standing in the middle of it like a figure in a clock. He'll stand there. He'll say that line, and rest his hand on that chair, and the next line is waiting a thousand years away, and he cannot reach for it until a reader turns the page.

Wicker walks sideways, to the left, to see how far you can go before the Count's eyes follow. They don't follow.

“He can't see us properly.”

“He's held at this passage,” Permancer says, very quietly. “It lets the lesson enter without changing what he does next. He's *fixed*. That's the courtesy of it. It means we can't harm him, and he can't harm us.”

“You've pinned him,” says Wicker.

“Wicker. Put the pen away.”

But the pen's already down. It's in the gutter of the book, in the crease, in the seam between worlds, and Wicker's got that bright, terrible, helpful look on his face, the look he wears when he's about to be clever at the one moment cleverness is no use. He glances once toward the door, the way you'd glance toward someone who's no longer there. Then he writes.

*For one sentence, let him choose the verb.*

The table draws in its legs. I feel that through the ribbon. The chairs move back a little, politely, the way furniture does in a dream, and the orange rolls off the end of the board and into the dark, and where it falls there's a sound like a very small door.

Dracula looks at Wicker.

Then, slowly, at *you.*

Then at the light that's behind you, the faint red thread of the ribbon, running back through the crease to where I am.

“What follows?” he asks.

He asks it exactly the way a man asks a question he already knows the answer to, and has just discovered he might be allowed to hear.

choices.title: Tell Wicker to cross it out.
choices.prompt: Tell Wicker to cross it out.
choices.result:
“Cross it out. *Now*, Wicker.”

Wicker's nib bites the paper and drags down through the sentence in one hard stroke. It tears the page. The tear runs a finger's width and stops, as if somebody on the other side has put out a hand.

The words hold anyway. They don't even flicker.
choices.braidText: You told Wicker to cross out his sentence. His nib tore the page, but the words held.

castMemories.memory: The reader told Wicker to cross out his sentence. His nib tore the page, and the words held anyway.
castMemories.aside: You told me to cross it out. I did. Hard. It didn't care. Ink's got no conscience, apparently.

choices.title: Call Permancer.
choices.result:
“Professor. *Professor.*”

Permancer is already turning, and he's already pulling the ribbon, with long slow draws of his whole arm, the way you'd haul a sail. He doesn't look surprised. He looks like a man who's been waiting for this exact sound since half past ten.
choices.braidText: You called Permancer. He was already pulling the ribbon.

castMemories.memory: The reader called for Permancer inside Dracula, and he was already hauling on the ribbon.
castMemories.aside: You called me. I was already pulling. I'd been listening for that sound since half past ten.

choices.title: Watch Dracula.
choices.result:
You don't speak. You don't breathe. You *watch,* because someone ought to.

His hand stays on the chair. It stays exactly where the paragraph put it. But his shadow, the long one, behind him on the wall, lets go of it and begins, very quietly, to move on its own.
choices.braidText: You watched Dracula. His hand stayed on the chair; his shadow let go.

castMemories.memory: The reader kept watching Dracula while everyone else moved, and saw his shadow let go of the chair.
castMemories.aside: You watched him. I should've been watching too. I was busy with knots.

castMemories.memory: Inside Dracula, Wicker wrote one sentence into the gutter of the book: for one sentence, let him choose the verb.
castMemories.aside: I gave him one verb. One. I keep doing the sum and it keeps coming out wrong.

castMemories.memory: Inside Dracula, Penny closed her hand on the Book's cover and told it to put its edges away.
castMemories.aside: The Book leaned at an orange inside Dracula. I told it to put its edges away. It did. Eventually.

nodes.title: Every named traveller
nodes.body:
The chandelier burns black. I don't know how else to say it. Every candle goes out at once and the whole fixture turns dark so completely that it's like a hole in the room, and out of the hole comes a small, thin, silken sound, which is the sound of a rule being broken somewhere you can't see.

“Penny. *Through.*” Permancer's voice has stopped being the voice of a lecturer. It's got no ornaments on it at all. “You next.”

You feel the ribbon. It's *warm* now, and it's alive, and it's tugging, and I do the only thing I can do, which is hold. I pull the line toward the Vault with every inch of my spine, and something snags against my stitching on the way, a loose, small, black thing, and I don't stop to look. I leave it where it is. I need both covers for this.

Penny reaches the light, and goes into it, and is gone. You follow. It isn't hard. That's the worst of it. The way home is the easiest thing in the world, a single red thread through the dark, and all you have to do is keep going.

You keep going.

It's the same road backward. The words come up under your feet, and they're the same words, but they feel different going the other way: not rushing, not racing, just *carrying,* the way a river carries a leaf it's decided to keep. The sound of the page turning's gone high and sweet. The smell of cold brass gives way, slowly, to the smell of the Vault: damp stone, old lamp-oil, a faint tang of tea.

Behind you, Wicker's backing toward the doorway with his pen in his fist.

“I gave you one verb,” he says.

He says it to the dark, like a boy explaining a mistake to a wall.

And Dracula, who's stood so still, so polite, so *held*, for a hundred years of Sundays, smiles, and says the only word he's been given the freedom to choose.

“Follow.”

Wicker crosses. Permancer holds the way open behind him, braced in the crease with both arms, the book pressing in at his shoulders.

“Back through. All of you. *Now.*”

The words reach farther than the ribbon. That's the last thing I know of the other side: a single long black word, curling after us across the floor like a lit fuse.

And then the professor's home, and the source slams shut behind him with a boom like a door in a cathedral.

The Vault's very quiet.

Penny runs her finger slowly down the list, and at every name, the matching ribbon *answers,* with a tiny twitch of silk. Every ribbon. Every name. She goes all the way to the bottom and then back to the top, to be sure.

“Complete,” she says.

Wicker sits down on the floor. There's ink on his knee, a long dark stripe, as if he's been kneeling in the gutter of something. He doesn't wipe it. He just looks at it, quietly, the way you look at a thing you can't take back.

He's gone quiet. It's not like him. I'd like to tell you it's all right, but I don't know yet that it is.

At supper he asks where Serenity is.

“Finishing her map,” Ambrose says. He's ladling the soup out as if it were any other night. “The East Stacks.”

Wicker takes the bowl Ambrose gives him. He holds it in both hands. By the time he lifts the first spoonful, it's gone cold.

Later, when the Kitchens have emptied, I go back through my stitching, thread by thread, along my spine, looking for the thing that snagged on the way home: a small black loose word with a long tail. I'd meant to keep it. I thought it might be a verb.

It's gone.

castMemories.memory: Back in the Vault, Penny ran her finger down the list and every ribbon answered. She said complete.
castMemories.aside: Complete. I said it out loud, so it was true. I checked it again after supper anyway.

nodes.title: This side of the cover
nodes.body:
You stayed in the Vault, and I kept your place.

That's a lesson too. Somebody has to be on this side of the door, and it's not a small job. It's the job of knowing where the way home *is.*

You stood with the doors and the cold while the others went into the book and the lamp hummed over the lectern. At some point Permancer's ribbon went taut across the flags, and a long thin sound came out of the open pages, and a few minutes later the whole room breathed out. It was a good, strong, tired sound. It was the sound of four people walking home.

Later, Penny brings the Club's report to where you're sitting, and sets it down beside you like a plate.

*On Sunday, Professor Permancer took the Book Jump Club into Dracula, a supervised visit to the entrance hall and no further. Wicker wrote one sentence in the source, giving the Count a choice of verb. The professor brought every named traveller home. Penny checked the list twice. Afterwards, a word was found missing from the Book's stitching.*

“It's a short report,” she says. “I'm told that's what's wanted.”

She looks at me then, and she looks at the place along my spine where the thread is loose.

“Don't poke it,” she says.
nodes.braidText: You stayed outside the visit. Later, Penny reported that every named traveller had returned from Dracula. A word caught in my stitching had gone missing.

castMemories.memory: The reader stayed in the Vault during the Jump, and Penny brought them the Club's report afterwards.
castMemories.aside: You held the Vault while we went in. Somebody has to know where the door is. You did. I wrote that down.

castMemories.memory: Permancer told the class that the reader staying in the Vault was a real part of the lesson.
castMemories.aside: You stayed on this side. Good. I'd like more people to know that's allowed.

storyScenes.title: The East Stacks Incident
storyScenes.opening:
A book lands in Ambrose's soup.

It comes out of nowhere, from somewhere above the rafters, and it hits the pot with the heavy slap of a very good hardback landing flat. Soup goes up in a brown arc. Everybody in the Kitchens ducks. Ambrose doesn't. He puts out one arm, takes the book out of the pot by the spine, like a man retrieving a drowned cat, and holds it up to the light.

*Doors That Should Stay Metaphors.* It drips on his shoes.

Then another book falls in the hall outside. Then another, farther away.

I don't like how they're falling. I know a thing or two about how books go over. They go over like that when someone's passed them in a great hurry, and the someone was very frightened, or very hungry, or both. They go over in a line. They go over in the order they were run past.

Ambrose puts down the ladle.

That's the moment I understand something is wrong. Ambrose Trencher doesn't put down the ladle. Not for the end of the world; I've heard him say so.

We follow the books. You carry me down the corridor at a half-run, and I try to keep very still against your ribs. The East Stacks are at the end of it: three floors of shelving, the oldest part of the library. They've done something I've never seen them do. They've squeezed their aisles shut. They've pushed in, shelf against shelf, like a held breath, and the only way through is sideways.

Penny Blackletter goes sideways. She goes with a catalogue card in each hand, following a trail of them. They're lying along the floor in a line, one after another, as if somebody's been dropping them out of a pocket. She picks one up and reads it and doesn't say a word, and then she reads the next, and I can see her mouth go flat.

All of them say the same thing, in the same bad, hurried hand.

HE WAS HERE.

“Serenity?” she calls.

Nothing. The shelves creak. A single book slides out of its place and falls into the dark.

“*Serenity.*”

Ambrose reaches the gap first. He's a big man and he shouldn't fit, and he fits. He kneels in a space no wider than a coffin, between *Travel* and *Unreliable Geography,* and puts his hand on the floor like someone checking a stove.

Serenity Brown is lying against the bottom shelf with her knees drawn up. Her map is open on the boards beside her, pinned under her elbow, as if even now she wouldn't let it go. She looks very small. Her collar's pulled aside. There are two small wounds at her neck, neat and dark and very close together, and I know exactly what they are, and I wish with my whole spine that I didn't.

I shut.

I didn't decide to. It's what covers do. You've seen a snail do it, and a hand, and a flower in the dusk. One second I'm open to the page and the next I've snapped closed like a mouth, hard enough that your fingers jump, and I can't open again. I try. I just can't.

“She's breathing,” Ambrose says. His voice is low and perfectly level. “Bring a clean cloth. And water. And then bring more water.”

Wicker turns so sharply he hits the shelf with his shoulder. A cascade of books slides off the top and he doesn't even look. He's gone. He comes back with three cloths over one arm and an empty water jug, and he stands there with it, looking at the jug, as if it had been handed to him by a stranger. Then he turns without a word and goes away again.

“Don't touch anything on the floor,” says Permancer, from the end of the aisle. “Don't touch *her.*” He's got the bookmark out. It's pulling in his fingers like a dowsing rod, bending toward Serenity, and then, shuddering, away from her toward the wall. “A living anchor.”

Penny catches his sleeve. “Explain.”

“He's holding on to her.” Permancer looks at the shelf. His face is grey and exact. “A person from a story has used her to stay. As long as he's got something in this world to hold, he doesn't fade. He's holding himself here by *her.*”

“I gave him—” Wicker begins, from behind us, with the jug.

“Water first,” says Ambrose.

Wicker stops. He crosses the last yard on his knees and sets the jug down by her hand without spilling a drop, and he doesn't look at her face. He looks at the jug.

Serenity opens her eyes.

They're very clear. They go to the ceiling, to the shelves, to the five of us bent over her, and then she frowns, and a small furious line appears between her brows.

“Will someone,” she says, “*please* stop turning that page?”

The shelves hold still. Everything in the East Stacks is closed. The books are all shut. I'm shut. I checked.

She doesn't seem to hear the answer. She's listening to something else, with her head a little on one side, the way you'd listen for a kettle in another room, and her hand goes out across the floor for the edge of her map.

choices.result:
You push her map nearer, an inch at a time, along the dusty boards, and her fingers find the edge of it and close.

Her hand knows where the map is, the way your tongue knows where a missing tooth used to be.

castMemories.aside: Somebody pushed my map to me in the Stacks. I know it was you. My hand remembers, even if the rest of me was busy.

choices.title: Offer Penny's pencil.
choices.result:
You take Penny's pencil out of her pocket, and Penny, to her enormous credit, lets you. You put it in Serenity's hand.

She draws one short, firm line on the map's edge, stops, and points the pencil at the north wall, which is just a wall, with nothing on it.

castMemories.aside: You gave me a pencil when I could barely see. I drew one line. It was the right line.

castMemories.memory: The reader took Penny's pencil out of her pocket to give to Serenity, and Penny let them.
castMemories.aside: You took my pencil. I let you. I'd like it known that I don't, as a rule, let anyone.

choices.result:
You set down your own breath and start moving books. You lift the fallen ones off the floor, a few at a time, and stack them where they won't slide.

Ambrose gets in beside her without stepping on the map, and he doesn't say thank you. He just shifts, a very little, to leave you the best of the light.

castMemories.aside: Put the ladle down. Don't make a thing of it.

castMemories.memory: Wicker ran for water, came back holding an empty jug, went again, and set it by Serenity's hand without spilling a drop.
castMemories.aside: I fetched an empty jug. All the way there and back. Empty. Ambrose said water first, so I went again.

castMemories.memory: Permancer's bookmark pulled toward Serenity, and he named it: a living anchor. Someone from a story was holding on to her.
