nodes.title: The East Stacks Incident
nodes.body:
“His fingers were coming apart,” Serenity says.

She says it to the ceiling. Her voice is scraped and quiet, but she gets every word out whole.

“He was *fading.* I could see right through his hand to the shelf. I told him he shouldn't be here. He said...” She stops, and her mouth twists. “He said he'd found a way to stay.”

She turns her head and looks at the cloth in Ambrose's hand, and at the water, and at the whole careful ring of us.

Wicker sets the jug down. A little water spills, and he wipes it up at once with his own sleeve, fast, before anyone can look at him. It's a ridiculous thing to be careful about. It's the only thing he's got hold of.

Serenity sees.

“What did you write?”

Nobody's expecting the question. Wicker looks up. For the first time since the shelf, his face is completely bare. He tells her. He gives her the whole sentence, word for word, in a flat steady voice, the exact words in the exact order, and I keep it too. I put it away carefully in the part of my stitching where I keep the things I can't forget.

She shuts her eyes.

He starts to reach for her hand. He gets halfway. Then he stops, and lays his own hand flat on the floor between them, and keeps it there.

“Get my map,” she says to Ambrose, without opening her eyes.

Ambrose gets the map.

And the Kitchens door appears at the end of the aisle.

It's come a long way. It's left its wall behind it and walked, in its own slow, wooden, loyal way, down three corridors and across a staircase, and now it stands in the gap between the shelves with soup on its lintel, ready to be used. Ambrose lifts Serenity, in one smooth movement, as if she weighed nothing, and she keeps the map. She keeps hold of it all the way.

On its surface, as it opens in her lap, a black line is moving.

It's thin, like a hair, and it crosses the little sea she drew, and goes up the river, and climbs the pencilled mountain, and slips off the edge of the map into the north margin. She didn't draw it. It's *tracing something.* Something is walking across her paper.

Serenity turns her head, just slightly, toward the wall.

“He's there.”

Permancer takes one step toward the north wall.

“Tomorrow,” Serenity says.

He stops.

“Yes,” says the professor, after a moment. “Tomorrow.”

Wicker holds the Kitchens door. He's the one who gets to it first. He stands with one hand on the frame and the other on the handle, very straight, like a doorman at an embassy, and Serenity is carried through it without a single look in his direction.

He stays at the handle long after Ambrose has set her down inside. He's got a death-grip on it. I notice that the wood has started to creak.

When we reach the Kitchens, there's already a paper bird on the bench by the place where they've laid her. It's folded very small, with nothing written on either wing. Soren isn't there. Nobody saw him come in, and nobody will say they saw him leave.

You're still here. I checked twice.

I don't like this aisle now. I'm going to remember exactly where it is, every shelf and every turning, so that we can never come back to it by accident.
nodes.braidText: Ambrose carried Serenity to the Kitchens. She kept her map. Wicker held the door; she passed without looking at him. I remembered the aisle.

castMemories.memory: Lying in the East Stacks, Serenity asked Wicker what he'd written in Dracula, and he told her the whole sentence, word for word.
castMemories.aside: She asked what I wrote. I told her. Exactly. It's the only thing I've done right all month, and it was just reading aloud.

castMemories.memory: Serenity was carried through the Kitchens door past Wicker, who was holding it, and she didn't look at him.
castMemories.aside: Everyone keeps telling me Wicker held the door. I know. I was there. I was busy holding the map.

castMemories.memory: Ambrose carried Serenity out of the East Stacks to the Kitchens. She kept hold of her map the whole way.
castMemories.aside: She kept the map the whole way. Wouldn't let me carry that too.

castMemories.memory: When Permancer stepped toward the north wall, Serenity said tomorrow, and he stopped.
castMemories.aside: She said tomorrow, and I stopped. I'd like to say it was wisdom. Mostly she said it first.

storyScenes.report: Penny left a report. Serenity was found in the East Stacks with two wounds at her neck. Ambrose carried her to the Kitchens. The Count had used her as a living anchor, and her map now traced where he went. Wicker brought water and held the door.

storyScenes.title: Leave me something to hold
storyScenes.opening:
Before we go anywhere else, I want to ask you for something small.

It's a strange thing to need, a small thing, after everything the Academy's about to throw at us. But I've been watching Permancer tie knots all week, and here's what I've noticed. A rope's only as good as what it's tied to.

My ribbon's been tied to *me.* I'm a perfectly decent anchor. But I'm only a book. I'm made of the same paper as every other book in the Labyrinth, and a door that leads into a story will always, eventually, find a way to turn me into one more page.

What I'd like is something that's real. Something that's *here.*

So look around you, wherever you are. Don't hunt for something grand. The chipped rim of your cup. The sound the fridge makes in the second before it stops. A mark on the back of your hand you've never been able to explain. The way the light comes in at four o'clock and lies down on the floor like a cat.

Pick one thing, and look at it for as long as it takes. Then give me a sentence I could find it by.

I'll hold that end of the rope. It's going to be useful. I can't promise you what for.
storyScenes.missionInvitation: Notice one thing near you. Bring back one true sentence.
storyScenes.missionReturnPrompt: The thing, exactly as you noticed it.
storyScenes.braidText: You brought back a sentence about something near you. I have that end.
storyScenes.missionKeptResponse: I've got it. We can go to some very strange places with something as particular as that tied to us.

storyScenes.title: The map with room left
storyScenes.opening:
Soren Ng comes into the Kitchens carrying a roll of tracing paper, the way you'd carry a sleeping animal.

It's raining, and he's carefully not dripping on it. He's got his sleeves rolled up past the wrist and a smudge of blue ink on his chin that nobody has told him about, and he stops just inside the door, as if the room might need a moment to adjust to him.

Serenity's at the long table. She's been out of bed for three days and she's been making toast. Not eating it; building with it. There's a tower rising on the bread-board in front of her, constructed from heels and crusts, held together with butter and ambition, and it's leaning very slightly to the left. She's named it Permancer.

“It's falling over,” says Ambrose, going past with a tray.

“He's *leaning,*” Serenity says. “It's different.”

Soren waits until the tower's decided to stay up. Then he comes to the table and puts the paper down beside her elbow, and weights the corners with the salt, the pepper, and an apple.

“I've copied the coast,” he says.

I feel the room change. It's tiny, a small tightening in the air, the way a window closes. Serenity's face goes still. Everything in her goes carefully shut.

“For the investigation?”

“For the boat.”

He unrolls it, and for a moment nobody speaks.

It's her boat. He's drawn it six times. It's the lentil-sized boat from the lunch-table map, with its flag, and he's put it into six harbours, each of them tiny and exact and wildly impossible. There's a harbour in the curl of a teacup. There's a harbour in a lighthouse lamp, where the boat's safe in the glass and the flame's a sunrise behind it. There's one beneath a bridge, one inside a bell, one in the font of a drowned cathedral. And the last is in a tree. It's a proper harbour, with a quay and a customs-house and a gull, and it's in the high crook of a very large oak, with the boat tied up at a branch.

Serenity looks at it for a long time.

She doesn't smile. Not yet. She puts out one finger and touches the tree.

“It'll need a ladder.”

“I wasn't sure how tall.”

“Taller than that.”

She holds out a hand, without looking at him, and he puts his pencil in it. It's a good pencil, soft, with a worn-down end, and she takes it as though it's the most natural thing in the world to be handed a pencil by this boy.

I start to close, out of politeness. She's about to draw and I don't want to be in the way.

She slides one finger between my leaves.

“Stay,” she says. “We need a cliff.”

So I stand on my fore-edge, upright, balanced between the salt and the bread-board, with my spine to the wall and my pages open like a very tall, very narrow country. And Serenity Brown draws a ladder up the side of me, rung by rung, in soft careful strokes, with her tongue between her teeth. It tickles. It tickles the whole way up.

“Hold still,” she tells me.

I've never held so still in my life.

That's when Wicker arrives.

He's in the doorway with a map case under his arm. It's *her* map case. It's the one that was damaged in the East Stacks, the leather torn at the corner, the clasp bent flat. It's been mended. Somebody has cut the damaged corner away and fitted a new piece of brass, small and sharp and clean, set at a very slightly crooked angle. It looks like the work of someone who's got no business doing it, and has done it anyway, and has been up all night.

He sees Soren's paper.

He sees six harbours, and a boat, and a ladder going up the side of a book.

I watch him look at the case. I watch him look at the harbours. Then, quite deliberately, he turns the case so that the repair faces his coat and the plain leather faces the room.

Ambrose takes it out of his hands. That's the only word for it. He simply removes it, the way you'd take a coat off a man who's about to walk into the sea.

“Tea?”

“No.”

“Then stop standing in the draught.”

Wicker takes a seat at the far end of the table. It's the farthest end. It's practically in the next room.

He sits there for the whole of one cup of tea, and the cup is the *entire* length of the thing, from the first pour to the last cold sip, and in all that time he doesn't say one word about Soren's harbours.

I've known Wicker Eddies to say nothing before. It's never lasted that long.
storyScenes.prompt: Six harbours for a little boat.
storyScenes.braidText: Soren brought Serenity a map for her boat. Wicker arrived with a repaired map case and stayed for tea. I stood on my fore-edge while she drew a ladder.

castMemories.memory: Soren brought Serenity tracing paper with her little boat drawn into six harbours, the last one up an oak tree.
castMemories.aside: Six harbours. She said the tree needs a ladder. She's right. I'm drawing a taller one.

castMemories.memory: Serenity drew a ladder up the side of the Book, standing on its fore-edge, so Soren's oak-tree harbour could be reached.
castMemories.aside: The Book held still while I drew a ladder up it. It tickled. It told me so. Several times.

castMemories.memory: Three days out of bed, Serenity built a tower of toast crusts in the Kitchens and named it Permancer. It leaned.
castMemories.aside: He's not falling over. He's leaning. It's different.

castMemories.memory: Wicker mended Serenity's torn map case overnight with a new brass clasp, then turned the repair toward his coat when he saw Soren's harbours.
castMemories.aside: I mended a map case. It took all night. Nobody's said thank you, which is fine, because nobody's supposed to know.

castMemories.memory: Ambrose took the mended map case out of Wicker's hands and made him sit down for a cup of tea.
castMemories.aside: Took the case off him before he walked into the sea with it. Gave him tea. Not a word for the whole cup.

storyScenes.title: The Man Reading Himself
storyScenes.opening:
“That one,” says Serenity.

She doesn't need the map to say it. She's got it open on her knee, and the black line on it has stopped wandering, and for the first time since the East Stacks it's pointing straight at a door.

It's the old reading-room door. It's always been shut; nobody's ever found the key. Tonight it's standing open about a hand's width, and a thin green light is lying along the floor of the corridor, and the corridor's *warm.* You can feel it on your face. People have been going in all week to get warm, and coming out thinking about something else.

We go in, the four of us: Serenity, Penny, you, and me.

The room is old in the way a cellar is old, quietly and all at once. Armchairs stand about with their stuffing coming out. Dust lies on everything like a patient grey animal. And in the centre, under a green-shaded lamp, in the best chair, with his long legs crossed and his hands folded round a book, sits Count Dracula.

He's reading *Dracula.*

I can see the spine from here. It's a copy of the very book we jumped into, black-bound and cracked. He holds it as though it were his own diary, and I suppose, in a way, it is.

He's got a pencil.

I dislike that before he's done anything with it. A man with a pencil in a library is a man with plans.

In the margin, beside a paragraph, he has written, in a small neat hand:

> He wouldn't have said this.

Penny leans round the doorframe.

“You wrote that?”

“I was present.” He doesn't look up. His voice is low and courteous, and carefully empty of any contraction, like a man polishing every word before he sets it down. “I have a better memory of the evening than the author did.”

“You can still be wrong.”

“I can,” says Dracula. “It would be a novelty.”

Serenity steps into the light.

He looks up then. He's very pale in the green. His eyes are the colour of the inside of a well, and for a moment, just a moment, something in them looks quite desperately tired. He rises. He does it carefully, the way very old men do, and he inclines his head.

“Miss Brown.”

“Serenity.”

He says it again, correctly. He doesn't hurry. She waits, with her map open on her arm and her chin up, and her bandage showing white at the edge of her collar.

Dracula sets the pencil down on the arm of the chair.

“I have read the last page,” he says.

His hand rests on the closed half of the book, the long half that's been turned over, the half that's finished.

“Every morning returns me to a sentence I have already lived. I wake at the same words. I cross the same room. I have said the same thing, and been answered, and been *afraid*, ten thousand times, in the same order, as if somebody had pressed me between two sheets of glass. You leave a room, and something can happen to you.” He lifts his eyes to hers. “I leave mine because the next paragraph says I must.”

“So you hurt me,” says Serenity.

“I was disappearing.”

“You knew I was a person.”

He looks at her bandage. For a long time he says nothing at all, and the lamp ticks, and the dust settles, and the warm of the room sits on us like a hand.

“Yes,” he says.

choices.prompt: “What would you do with a tomorrow?”
choices.result:
“What would you do with a tomorrow?”

He turns the pencil between his fingers, slowly, end over end. For once it's the whole of his attention. “Something I have not read,” he says.

“That's an empty answer,” says Serenity.

He lays the pencil down again. He doesn't argue. That's the strangest thing about him.

castMemories.aside: You asked him about tomorrow. Good question. Empty answer. I'd still ask it again.

choices.title: “Why her?”
choices.result:
“Why her?”

“She saw me.” His voice is low. “A witness holds a man still for a moment. I made that moment last.”

Serenity pulls the chair out from the other side of his little table, and sits in it, and folds her hands over her map. He has to look at her now. It's an odd thing to watch: a vampire being looked at, properly, for the first time in a century.
choices.braidText: You asked Dracula why Serenity. He said witnessing held him briefly, and he made it last. She sat opposite him.

castMemories.memory: The reader asked Dracula why Serenity. He said she saw him, and Serenity sat down across the table and made him look at her.
castMemories.aside: You asked why me. He said I saw him. So I sat down and made him look back.

choices.title: “Would you do it again?”
choices.result:
“Would you do it again?”

The lamp buzzes. Nobody breathes.

“If I were vanishing?” says Dracula. “Yes.”

Penny writes the word down. She writes it plainly, in her smallest hand, and she doesn't offer him a softer one.
choices.braidText: You asked Dracula whether he would do it again. He said yes if he were vanishing. Penny wrote his answer.

castMemories.memory: The reader asked Dracula whether he'd do it again. He said yes, if he were vanishing, and Penny wrote the word down plainly.
castMemories.aside: You asked if he'd do it again. He said yes. I wrote it in my smallest hand. It still took up the whole page.

castMemories.memory: In the old reading room, Serenity faced Dracula and made him say he'd known she was a person when he hurt her.
castMemories.aside: He said yes. He knew I was a person. I wanted it said out loud. Now it has been.

castMemories.memory: Penny caught Dracula writing in the margin of his own book that he wouldn't have said this.
castMemories.aside: He was annotating himself. In pencil. I've met students like that. None of them were vampires.

nodes.title: The Man Reading Himself
nodes.body:
Dracula opens his book.

He turns to the last page, the very last, and runs one finger down it as though it's a bill.

“I want a future tense,” he says. “Yours has been waiting for you all day.”

It's a very simple sentence, and it fills the room. Something goes cold in me. I think it's the thread in my spine.

“And if it costs someone else?” Penny asks. She's got her pencil out. Her voice is flat and quite steady.

“I intend to remain.”

That's all. It sounds like the courteous refusal of a man declining a second helping.

Serenity stands. She doesn't hurry. She folds her map shut with one hand, flips the clasp, and lets it click.

“Then we'd better learn how to send you back.”

His shadow moves first.

It does it before he does. It goes up the wall, long and quick and independent, and reaches the nearest shelf, and *opens* it. I don't mean it opens a door. It opens a book. One of the old volumes on the shelf falls wide, and out of it comes the sea, a grey wind-driven sea with a boat on it, tilting, and the smell of salt and tar rolls across the room like a wave. Another book opens, and snow comes in, real snow, small and dry, and settles on the arms of the chairs. A third lets in roses. They push their dark red heads through the pages and one of them catches on Penny's sleeve.

Dracula steps backward, between them.

For a moment, he's standing in three doorways at once. The sea's behind him, and snow's on his shoulders, and roses are growing round his hand, and he looks, in each of them, like a different man. A sailor. A traveller. A suitor. He looks at Serenity from all three of them.

Then the books close, in the same instant, with a sound like a single breath.

The room is empty. The chair is still warm. The snow on the arm of it melts as we watch.

Serenity unfolds her map. It takes her a moment. The black line, which has run straight as a ruled stroke since the East Stacks, has split. It's branched, twig and twig and twig, like frost on a window, a hundred thin paths racing off the page in every direction.

Penny pulls a thorn from her cuff and holds it up to the lamp.

“How many ways?”

“More than yesterday,” says Serenity.

I keep the fallen thorn. I take it between my pages, very carefully, so it can't hurt anyone. It came out of a book, and it can still scratch you, and I think that's a good thing to be reminded of.
nodes.braidText: Dracula wanted a future tense. Serenity said they must learn to send him back. His shadow opened several books, and the black line on her map branched.

castMemories.memory: Dracula escaped the old reading room through three opened books, and the black line on Serenity's map split into a hundred branches.
castMemories.aside: The line on my map's gone everywhere. More ways than yesterday. I said that. It's still true.

castMemories.memory: A rose caught Penny's sleeve as Dracula escaped through the books, and she pulled the thorn out and held it to the lamp.
castMemories.aside: A rose came out of a book and caught my sleeve. The Book kept the thorn. I'd have filed it under evidence.

storyScenes.report: Penny recorded the meeting in the old reading room. The Count wanted a future beyond his written ending. Serenity faced him about the harm he'd done. He escaped through several books, and the black line on her map split into branches.

storyScenes.title: An Invitation Without Words
storyScenes.opening:
I've been watching the chair Ambrose leaves pulled back.

It's the one beside Serenity's map. It's been out from the table every lunch for weeks, and nobody's sat in it, and still the whole room's been arranged around it. People walk the long way. Conversations leave a little gap. When somebody new comes in, their eyes go to it before they've even said hello, and a kind of understanding passes over their face, and they sit.

It hasn't got a sign. It hasn't got a word on it. And it's saying *come in,* as plainly as a bell.

That's the thing I want to know about. Not the chair. The *saying.*

Somewhere near you right now, something is inviting somebody in. A lamp left on in a window. A path worn into the grass, and everybody following it without being told. A gate that's been propped open with a brick. A place at a table, set for one more.

Find it. Stand in front of it for a minute. Notice how it does it.

Then give me one sentence about how it invited you. You can leave the thing where it is. It's not going anywhere. I only want to carry the sentence.
storyScenes.missionInvitation: Find something that says come in without words. Bring back one true sentence.
storyScenes.braidText: You brought back a sentence about something that invited you in without words.
storyScenes.missionKeptResponse: I can work with that. The Academy keeps drawing doorways. You've brought me an invitation.

storyScenes.title: The Wrong Castle
storyScenes.opening:
The East Stacks grow a tower overnight.

You can see it from the Great Hall windows when the morning mist comes off: a thick dark finger standing where the library's east wing used to end. The bottom of it is *library.* It's got the right stone, the right narrow windows, the right smell of old glue. About halfway up, it changes its mind. There's a stretch of grey fortress wall with a flag on it that's no flag the Academy owns. And at the very top, as if the tower couldn't stop itself, there's a nursery window with yellow curtains and a wooden star hanging in the glass.

Between them runs a stair, and the stair keeps asking for another floor.

I can hear it from here. It's a slow soft *tick,* like a clock being wound. Each time the stair asks, the tower takes a stone from somewhere else and says yes.

A drawbridge hangs down over the Quillquarium. The nibs underneath are in a state. They've never agreed so completely, all thousand of them, in one long furious scribble, and the noise of it comes up through the floor like bees in a wall.

I've read about a tower like this one. It was in a book, and the book was careful, and the tower stayed in the book. It wasn't supposed to get out.

Penny's pinning up a notice on the foot of the stair. She does it with a drawing-pin and quite a lot of dignity:

> THE EAST STACKS ARE SEVERAL PLACES. PLEASE USE ONE AT A TIME.

Permancer is tying ribbons to the banister, one at every third post, in a pattern he's clearly worked out on paper. Wicker is holding the source volume, the old black copy of *Dracula,* open at the page, closed over his finger. He holds it like a man who's been handed a baby by an enemy. Serenity is studying her map.

It's been thirteen days since the East Stacks. She's gone back to her work. She's gone back to toast. She's lost no weight in the face and gained no softness, and on her neck, above the collar, there's a thin line that isn't quite scar and isn't quite not. She looks up from her map, and across the hall at the tower, and the corner of her mouth goes in.

“I'm coming,” she says.

“I was about to ask,” says Permancer.

“You're very slow.”

“I'm very thorough.”

“That's what I said.”

She folds the map into her repaired case. It's the mended one, with the small crooked clasp. I watch the clasp click shut under her thumb, a clean small *snick,* and I watch Wicker, across the hall, watch it happen. He watches it the way you'd watch a bridge you've built take weight for the first time.

She catches him looking.

She doesn't smile. She doesn't scowl. She gives him a small, level nod, just a fraction of an inch, the kind you give to a stranger who's held a door. Then she goes ahead.

Permancer counts us at the doorway. He counts twice, now. He's started to count a third time, and he stops himself, and just holds the bookmark a moment longer than he needs to, and nobody says anything.

Inside, the stair turns into a corridor. It's a long one, lamplit, with a floor of old boards and, beyond a bend, three ways through.

I tie my ribbon to the doorframe behind us. It's the only thing I can do. It's the end I've got, and I leave it fluttering there like a flag on a very small ship, so that, whatever else happens, we'll be able to find the way out.

choices.title: The ballroom.
choices.result:
You step into the ballroom, and the floor starts a waltz.

Your first step starts a waltz. Your second starts something with drums in it, a fast hot rhythm from a different century, and by your third the two have collided and the whole room's shaking itself like a wet dog. Dancers appear out of the walls: empty coats and gowns, full of nobody, wheeling past in the candlelight with their arms out.

You find the beat you can follow, and you cross to it. The coats sweep past you like a tide. One of them takes your hand and then, courteously, gives it back.
choices.braidText: You crossed the ballroom to a beat you could follow. Empty coats swept past.

choices.title: The nursery.
choices.result:
You push open the nursery door, and a wooden star on a string swings out of the dark and catches your sleeve.

You unhook it carefully. It's very light, painted blue, with one chipped point. As you hold it, it grows a tooth: one small grey tooth of stone, set into the lowest point, like a thing that's been dreaming of being a gargoyle.

You put it down gently on the window-sill. It looks hopeful.
choices.braidText: You unhooked a wooden star from your sleeve. It had grown one stone tooth.

choices.title: The red chair.
choices.result:
You choose the red chair, which sits alone in the middle of an otherwise empty passage, facing the wall. Four doors bring you back to it, one after another, each a little less apologetic than the last.

On the fifth time, Serenity strides across the floor, takes the chair by its back, and turns it around to face the wall.

“It wanted to be looked at,” she says. “Now it's got something to look at.”

The next door finally lets you through.
choices.braidText: You took the way through the red chair. Serenity turned it towards the wall, and the next door let you through.

castMemories.memory: In the borrowed castle, the red chair brought the reader back four times, until Serenity turned it to face the wall.
castMemories.aside: That chair kept bringing you back. It wanted looking at. So I gave it a wall. Problem solved.

castMemories.memory: Penny pinned a notice at the foot of the castle stair: the East Stacks are several places, please use one at a time.
castMemories.aside: My notice said one place at a time. Nobody's read it. The stair certainly hasn't.

castMemories.memory: Permancer counted everyone at the castle door twice, and nearly a third time.
castMemories.aside: I count twice now. I nearly counted three times at the castle. Penny saw. She didn't say. I'm grateful.

castMemories.memory: Wicker watched Serenity fasten the map case he'd mended, and she gave him a small, level nod.
castMemories.aside: She used the case. Closed it, click. Nodded at me. A whole nod. I'm not making anything of it.

castMemories.memory: Serenity caught Wicker watching her close her mended map case, and gave him a small, level nod before going ahead.

nodes.title: The Wrong Castle
nodes.body:
Dracula's waiting in the central hall.

It's a great high round room, built out of several different castles, and none of them has agreed to hold it up. The ceiling's from one place. The floor's from another. A fireplace in the north wall is blowing snow into the room, sideways, in long clean ribbons, and it's settling on the Count's coat. Above him, the stolen nursery window has swung in on its own wall, and is trying very hard to find morning.

“This is not my castle,” he says.

He sounds, for the first time, uncertain. He sounds like a man standing in somebody else's kitchen.

“No,” says Serenity. “These are everybody else's rooms.”

She's got her map in both hands, and her chin up.

A door opens in the east wall, and through it there's a small boat in a great storm, the whole sea heaving past the frame. Permancer throws himself at the handle and drags it shut, and a quart of seawater goes through the gap and soaks him to the knees.

“You have damaged my source,” says Dracula.

There's no heat in it. It's an accusation said very quietly, with a certain regret, by a man who's found his house wrecked and isn't sure whose fault it is.

Permancer keeps both hands on the handle. He's wet and he's tired and for once he's not lecturing.

“We did,” he says.

It's a big thing, to say. I feel it go through the room. Nobody's expecting it, least of all the Count.

Wicker's holding the source volume open. He's standing very still, his shoulders drawn in, looking down at the page. His own sentence is there, in his own hand. *For one sentence, let him choose the verb.* And under it, in a second hand, small and neat, one word:

*FOLLOW.*

“I thought—” Wicker begins.

Serenity waits. She doesn't help him. She just waits.

He looks at the map case, with its crooked clasp. At the bandage above it, half hidden by her collar. He looks, I think, at everything he's ever made go wrong.

“I wanted to see what would happen.”

“You have,” says Serenity.

It's not cruel. It's perfectly level. He takes it. He lowers his eyes to the page and, for the first time since the Jump, doesn't look away.

Then the wall splits.

It happens quietly. There's a long thin crack, as if a very big breath has been let out behind the plaster, and where the stone parts there's something white. It's a fold of paper. A single sheet, thin as a held breath, running up the wall like ivy.

I know that paper.

I'd know it in the dark. I'd know it from across the Labyrinth. It's the same stuff I'm made of: the same flax, the same lime, the same long slow soak in a vat. It's *paper.* It's a page. And there's a gap in the page, a narrow clean tear like the one in the corner of a bookplate, and cold air's coming through it, and through the cold I can *hear* something. It's very far off. It sounds like a cover being opened.

Serenity touches the fold with one finger. Her map pulls toward the gap in her hands, the whole sheet stretching toward it like a plant.

“His way back,” she says.

Permancer brings the bookmark near. Its ribbons lift, one by one, and reach across the hall toward the source volume in Wicker's hands, toward the tear in the wall, and, slowly, almost reluctantly, toward Serenity.

Penny's already got three cards out. She sets one beside each, with a click.

SOURCE. INVITATION. LIVING CLAIM.

Dracula watches her write. His face doesn't move.

Serenity looks at the third card. It lies on the flagstone by her foot, plain white, with her own name nowhere on it. Then she puts out her hand, flat, and covers it.

“That one's mine.”

Behind us, through the shut door, the sea knocks again.
nodes.braidText: In the borrowed castle, Penny named source, invitation, and living claim. Serenity put her hand over the third card. That one was hers.

castMemories.memory: In the castle's central hall, Wicker found FOLLOW written under his sentence, and told Serenity he'd only wanted to see what would happen.
castMemories.aside: I told her I wanted to see what would happen. She said I had. She wasn't wrong. She rarely is.

castMemories.memory: When Dracula said the Academy had damaged his source, Permancer answered: we did.
castMemories.aside: We did. Two words. It took me eleven years and a vampire to say them.

castMemories.memory: Penny laid three cards on the castle floor: source, invitation, living claim.
castMemories.aside: Three cards. It helps, writing a thing down. It's harder to be frightened of a word on a card.

castMemories.memory: Serenity put her hand flat over the card that said living claim. That one was hers.
castMemories.aside: Living claim. It's my name on that card, even if nobody wrote it. I'll be the one who lets go.

storyScenes.report: The East Stacks had become a tangle of borrowed rooms. In the central hall, Penny named three parts of the return: source, invitation, living claim. Serenity put her hand over the third card. Only she could withdraw that claim.

storyScenes.title: The other side
storyScenes.opening:
Penny's gone round the back of the chalk door.

She's been there a while. Permancer's followed her. I can hear the two of them back there, murmuring, in the voices of people who've just discovered a room in their own house.

It's a very simple thing to do. I don't know why it works.

Pick something you know well, something you've looked at a hundred times, from one side only. The mug. The chair. The front of your own front door. Turn it over. Walk behind it. Read the back of the thing you've been carrying around in your pocket.

You'll find that everything has two faces. One's the face it shows. The other's the face it *has.* They're hardly ever the same.

Tell me one sentence about what you couldn't see before.
storyScenes.missionInvitation: Look at something familiar from its other side. Bring back one sentence.
storyScenes.braidText: You looked at something familiar from another side and brought back a sentence about what you found.
storyScenes.missionKeptResponse: Oh. Keep that beside the first look. I want both.

storyScenes.title: Which preparation?
storyScenes.opening:
It's the night before the night.

Everyone in the Great Hall can feel it. The stair's still there between the supper tables, and the torches along the walls have started to lean toward it, and the benches are half empty, as if half the school has decided to be elsewhere. Those of us who stayed have been given work.

Three preparations are underway. I can only fit under one arm at a time.

Ambrose has laid a place at the end of the long table: a bowl, a spoon, a cup, a napkin folded just so. It's a proper place. Penny has chalk up to her elbows and a very small, very firm expression, and she's kneeling in the middle of the flags with a piece of string. nodes.title: Supper with a Finished Man
nodes.body:
Ambrose invites Dracula to supper.

He does it by pulling out a chair. That's all. He walks across the Great Hall in his apron, with the ladle in his belt and a damp tea-towel over his shoulder, and he stops in front of the vampire who's been standing in the doorway for the last ten minutes, and he pulls out a chair.

“In here?” says Penny, behind him, in a whisper that carries.

“The soup's in here.”

Dracula stops beside the chair. He doesn't sit.

“Your invitation is imprecise.”

“Sit down,” says Ambrose, “and we'll improve it.”

It's the whole of Ambrose Trencher's method, and I've seen it work on weeping first-years and furious professors and a goat. He never argues. He just puts food near you. He stands there with that great plain patient face, and the soup steams, and sooner or later whatever you came in to say seems a little less urgent than whatever's on the plate.

Serenity takes the place opposite. She's pulled her chair up very straight and put her map on the table beside her bowl, with its clasp shut. She doesn't look at the Count. She looks at the soup, with the polite hard attention of someone sitting down for the worst meal of her life.

Ambrose fills her bowl. He fills yours. He fills his own. He leaves Dracula's empty, and doesn't remark on it.

“You presume I do not eat.”

“What would you like?” says Ambrose.

Dracula looks at the soup. It's a good thick winter soup, with a skin of gold on the top, and I think, just for a moment, he really *looks* at it, the way you'd look through a window at a country you've left.

“Nothing,” he says.

Ambrose nods, as if that's an answer he knows how to work with, and passes the bread.

“I will not return to a finished life,” Dracula says. He says it as if reciting it. “I would rather be nothing in this world than a sentence in that one.”

Serenity sets down her spoon.

“You're staying,” she says, “by holding on to mine.”

He looks at her. She waits. It's a long look. She holds it until he is the one who turns his eyes away.

Ambrose gets up and goes to the dresser. He opens the recipe drawer. It's the old one, crammed with cards and torn corners and clipped sheets, all of them thumb-marked with forty years of butter, and he takes out a single sheet of paper with a clean fold. It's got a butter mark in one corner, the size of a thumb.

He lays it down on the table between the bowls.

I'd have found him a clean one. I'd have gone and looked for it. I think that's why he didn't ask me.

nodes.body:
They write the other terms beneath the first. It takes a long time, and nobody hurries. Penny reads each one back aloud. Permancer stands at the far end, silent, with his hands folded and his collar still damp from the sea. Dracula reads them all himself, with the point of one long finger, line by line.

“And in exchange, I go back.”

“And you let go,” says Serenity.

He puts a finger on the butter mark.

“This was a recipe.”

“It still is,” says Ambrose. He's putting more bread on the table. “We're trying to get everyone out of this room alive.”

The Count signs. His hand is slow and beautiful, and the signature goes across the page like a string of black beads. Permancer will add his name at the return.

Ambrose passes dessert around the table: a bowl of baked apple, spiced, with cream. He sets one down in front of every place. He sets one down, without a word, in front of Dracula's empty bowl.

Dracula's bowl stays empty.

I counted the spoons, all along. There's one out for him anyway.

nodes.title: The Door’s Autopsy
nodes.body:
Penny draws a chalk outline on the floor of the Great Hall, around the place where the door stood.

It's a very careful outline. She starts at the top and works down, kneeling on a folded coat, tongue between her teeth, and she goes round it twice. At the end she stands up and looks at it.

“No body,” she says. “Unhelpful.”

There *is* a body. It's the door. It's the only body in the case. Nobody ever counts doors, because a door's the thing you walk through to get to something else, and nobody turns round afterwards to ask what happened to it.

Permancer lays out the evidence in a row along the edge of the chalk: the roster, with its four names. The ribbon, with its knot. The source volume. Wicker's sentence, on its torn page. And Serenity's map, folded, with the black line threading across it like a hair. The professor's case is open beside them, and in the lid someone has pinned a small note in his own handwriting. *Back before supper.*

It's the saddest note I've ever read. It's from the day of the Jump.

nodes.title: The Door’s Autopsy
nodes.body:
The other cards follow, one at a time. The floorboards shift them. They creak, and slide, and slowly settle into a triangle, as if the whole Great Hall's leaning in to see.

I want to see it from above. It's a thing I've never been able to do; I'm not tall. Penny notices, and picks me up. She holds me over her head with both hands, like a lantern, and the triangle opens under me, three cards, three corners, one shape.

The chalk rises. It lifts off the floor in thin white lines and forms, in the air, the frame of a doorway. It's an ordinary doorway, with a lintel and two posts, quite empty, and the Great Hall shows through it.

{other-side}

From Penny's side of the door, the ribbons all point inward. It's only a small change. It's the difference between looking at a room from the street and looking at it from the hearth.

Permancer walks around to join her.

For a long time, he doesn't speak. He stands at her shoulder, and looks at the doorway he's stood facing his whole life, and sees it for the first time from the other side.

“I kept standing where I'd always stood,” he says.

Penny makes room for him. It's not much room. She just moves her elbow.

“Now you're here.”

He reads the cards backward, and then forward.

“Open his source,” he says slowly. “Give him an invitation he recognises. Serenity withdraws the claim. And then the source can take him back.”

“That's the shape of it,” says Penny.

The chalk door turns, very slowly, in the air. It rotates until it's facing the Great Hall's long table, and beyond the door, framed by the lintel, you can see a chair waiting, pulled back from the table, with nobody in it.

Penny takes a fourth card from her pocket. It's empty. She sets it down gently beneath INVITATION.

“Well,” she says. “We've got somewhere to start.”

nodes.title: A Room Made of Paper
nodes.body:
Wicker has covered the floor of the Great Hall in spoiled menus.

It's an enormous number. He's gone through every kitchen, every pantry, every office in the school, and taken every card and sheet and bill of fare that anybody's ever spilled something on. They lie in overlapping rows from one wall to the other, some stained, some torn, some with *Tuesday Special* in a hand that's been dead for fifty years.

“Blank on the back,” he says, before Penny asks.

All that blank. I have to sit on my own corner to stop myself looking at it. It's the loveliest sight I've ever seen: acre on acre of waiting paper, every sheet with its other side turned up like a hand.

A quill crawls out from under the first menu. It's a small black one, with a crooked nib, and it's clearly been living there. Wicker doesn't startle. He lifts the corner of the menu with two fingers and waits, politely, while it makes its way out. Then he lets the paper fall.

Serenity sits nearby, with her back against the leg of a table. Her map case rests against her ankle.

Wicker draws a room.

He does it with a stub of charcoal, in a few easy strokes, on the first clean surface. A floor, a ceiling, a door. When he's finished, he lifts the sheet carefully, and folds, and the room *rises:* a little paper chamber, standing up off the flags, cream-coloured and quiet and slightly bigger than it ought to be. Its first wall won't stand. It slumps.

“Stay flat, then,” he says to it, irritably.

It springs upright.

Penny writes something down.

“You needn't record that.”

“I may teach it,” she says.

He folds a second wall. His hands are quick and sure and perfectly clean. He's *good* at this. He's much better than he lets on, and the paper seems to know it. I think even the paper's annoyed.

Serenity leans forward. She's watching the room, not him.

“Your window's too high.”

“For whom?”

“Anyone who wants to see out.”

He looks at her. She waits. There's something almost like a smile in the corner of his mouth, and it vanishes, and he lowers the window. It's a small thing, a half-inch. Their eyes meet through the little opening, her face in the square of it, her hair, her chin, the line on her neck.

He looks down first.

“I could take the anchor,” he says, very low.

“No.”

“If it would—”

“No.” She says it gently, which is worse. “Fix the window.”

He folds the sill to the right height, with great care, and doesn't say another word.

nodes.title: A Room Made of Paper
nodes.body:
Behind the window, there's an unwritten night.

It's the loveliest thing in the room. It isn't dark, quite. It's the colour of a page before the ink gets to it, soft and open and waiting. A few small stars sit in it that Wicker hasn't drawn yet, or hasn't decided to, and I can feel them there, just under the surface, like words on the tip of the tongue.

He runs a long paper fold from the floor of the room out across the flagstones, and across the Great Hall, and up onto the lectern. It ends in the open pages of *Dracula.*

“When he enters,” he says, “we fold it back.”

“Wait for me,” Serenity says.

She says it quite quietly. She's not looking at the room. She's looking at him.

He nods, once. He tests the crease between finger and thumb, smooths it, and leaves the last fold open: one flap of paper, standing up from the rest like a door left ajar.

I watched where he left it. I'll know that fold again.

She watches his hands.

Far away, beyond the walls, a closed book stops turning its pages. I hear it stop. I think the others do, too. It's the particular silence of someone who's just been looked at.

Serenity's map stirs in her case. It pulls toward the paper room, toward the fold, with a small tug that moves the whole case across the floor.

“He's noticed,” she says.

nodes.braidText: Wicker made the paper room. Serenity told him to wait for her. He left the last fold open.

storyScenes.title: A Future Tense
storyScenes.opening:
The stair has reached the supper tables.

It came in the night, step by step, up from the East Stacks and along the Great Hall floor, and now its last tread rests quietly against the end of the long table, like a cat that's found the warm spot. Ambrose moves the salt out of its way. He does it without comment. He's moved a great deal of furniture this week for things that weren't furniture.

A paper moon hangs over the hall. It's a real moon, in its way: round and cold and the colour of skimmed milk, but it's been torn out of somebody's book, and you can see the ragged edge where it came loose. It hangs there, turning very slowly, and the whole room's lit by it, the sort of light that makes everything look like a drawing of itself.

On the wooden stand by the end of the table, the old black copy of *Dracula* is trying to close.

It's a slow, patient, terrible effort, like a man trying to shut a door with a crowd on the other side. The covers drag together by an inch, and are dragged apart. I know what it needs. It needs somebody to wedge in, and *hold.*

So I do it. I slide myself, spine first, beneath its front board, and I let the weight come down on me. It presses on my back like a hand. I've held open heavier books than this, I think. I can't remember when. I'm not certain I've held open anything at all.

Permancer reads the return list aloud. This time he names every one of us who's allowed through, slowly, every syllable in the right order, and he doesn't skip a name or say it twice. Penny checks every ribbon from both sides, leaning over the stand, and then crouching down to look at the underside, and then lying flat on the floor.

Serenity stands by the final fold. It's the one Wicker left open. The map case lies at her feet, wide open, with the map spread out in it like a patient. She isn't looking at anything. She's *listening,* with her head a very little on one side, and her hand goes up to the line on her neck and stops short of it.

“He's coming,” she says.

The paper moon goes dark.

The whole hall goes dark with it. And down the stair, one step at a time, with the unhurried courtesy of a man in his own house, comes Dracula.

He sees the open source. He sees Serenity. He sees the invitation we've made.

Ambrose pulls a chair back from the table. He does it slowly, with both hands. It's the one at the head, the one that's been laid for no one all week, and as it comes away from the board, something happens in the air. The threshold takes its shape from the empty place.

Dracula stops on the last stair.

He has noticed.

nodes.title: Return by Terms
nodes.body:
Ambrose brings the supper table to the threshold.

He does it alone. He gets his shoulder under one end and walks it across the flags with a long wooden scrape that makes the nibs in the Quillquarium shriek, and when he sets it down at the edge of the gap it wobbles. One leg's short. It's always been short. He takes a folded menu out of his apron and slides it under, and the table steadies.

I'm still wedged under the Count's cover. Nobody's put a menu under me.

Dracula crosses the last of the stair. He stops before the table, at a courteous distance, and looks down at the sheet laid out on it. It's the sheet from the supper. The butter mark's in one corner, and underneath it his own signature, the long black string of beads.

He reads it. He reads it slowly, as a man might read a will.

Permancer comes forward. He's put on a fresh collar. His hand shakes slightly as he takes up the pen, and he signs the Academy's admission beneath the Count's, in his own plain upright hand. *The door was opened, and its return was wrongly declared safe.* He signs it as if every letter cost him something.

“No promise of release,” says Dracula.

“None.”

“No visit.”

“None.”

“No second chance at the door.”

“None,” says Permancer, and puts down the pen.

The Count looks at Serenity. She's waiting beside the open source, with the map case at her feet, and her hands folded in front of her as though she were waiting for a train.

“Poor terms,” he says.

Ambrose puts a hand on the table to steady it. He doesn't look up.

“They're the ones you signed.”

The Count reads them again. It takes a long time, and the moon's gone out, and the only light is the faint grey pulse of the open book. Penny checks the ribbons. Wicker, at the final fold, holds the paper still between his fingers and doesn't breathe. I hold. My corner's gone numb. I've lost the feeling in my spine's whole left side.

Dracula turns from the table, and steps toward the threshold.

nodes.title: The claim is hers
nodes.body:
At the edge of the source, Dracula turns to Serenity.

“You would send me back.”

She unfolds her map. She does it slowly, so that everybody can see, flat across both hands, like a woman opening a letter she's already read. On it the black line runs from him across the room and across the sea, over the mountain, back down the river, and into the little kingdom she drew before any of this began. It's got a boat in it. It's got a flag.

“What you changed in me is mine now,” she says.

It's a quiet voice. It's perfectly clear. I think everyone in the Great Hall hears it, the whole row of benches, and the ribbons, and the moon.

She puts a finger beneath the line.

“It doesn't belong to you.”

The ink lifts. It comes up from the paper like a loose thread from a hem, thin and black and shining, and she holds it between finger and thumb, in the cold grey light, as lightly as she held the pencil at the lunch-table.

“It doesn't hold you here.”

She pulls it free.

It's a long moment. I've never heard a silence with so much in it. It's the silence of a very large thing being undone by a very small one, a single thread, drawn out of a cloth that's taken three hundred years to weave. His second shadow goes out first. It goes out like a lamp. The open book drags at his coat. It's got him by the hem, and the shoulders, and every one of the sleeves, and under my boards I feel the covers strain with the whole of the story.

I hold.

A stitch parts in my spine. It doesn't hurt. It's a very small sound, the sound of a thread going quietly in a seam, and then another, further down, and then a warm loose feeling like a drawer left open. I hold anyway. I'm not going to be the one to let him go.

Dracula looks into the source. He looks into it for a long time, at the dark gold lamplit hall with its table and its chandelier and its single chair. For once, he doesn't know what to say before the page turns.

It turns anyway.

**It's like this, going back.**

It sounds like a long exhale: the whole Labyrinth breathing out. It *smells* like cold brass again, and wet slate, and woodsmoke, and the first morning of the year. The stair breaks into words. It does it from the top down, one tread at a time, each step falling into a line of print and the print scattering, a black flock, up into the rafters, where it hangs a moment like starlings and settles into the dark between the beams. The ballroom sheds its extra centuries with a long rustling sound like silk coming off a body. The drawbridge lifts out of the Quillquarium with a flock of nibs still hanging from it, all of them shrieking, a hundred little black birds on a string, and every one of them stops, mid-scream, and goes quiet.

The borrowed moon sails back between two covers. It goes up in a slow white arc, with the edge of it dragging like a hem, and a book somewhere in the dark takes it in with a sound like a swallowed breath. The covers close over it. And the sky outside the Great Hall windows, which has been the wrong colour for a month, is suddenly the colour of an ordinary night, damp, blue-black, full of stars.

Then the Great Hall's a hall again.

I wriggle out from under *Dracula.* It's a bad moment: my loose stitch catches on the edge of the stand and pulls. Penny's there at once. She frees it with the point of her pencil, gently, one thread at a time, with her lips pressed together, like someone untangling a child's hair.

Serenity listens.

She stands very still. She holds the map in front of her, the black line gone, the paper clean, and her head's tilted a little, as it's been tilted for a fortnight. Somewhere very far away, past walls and shelves and a hundred shut doors, a closed book turns a page.

She lets out a breath.

She picks up her map case. She puts the map in it, folds the flap, and does up the little crooked clasp with one hand.

“Still there,” she says.

Ambrose pulls out a chair.

This time, it's for her.

Someone has left a paper bird on the banister at the foot of the stair. It's been there since dusk, with its wings folded, and nothing written on either of them. When Serenity sits, it drops down onto the lid of her map case, a quarter-inch from her hand, and she doesn't brush it off. On the underside of the right wing, in small blue letters: *whenever you want the long way.*

nodes.title: Return by Rule
nodes.body:
Penny places the cards around the opening.

She does it one at a time, kneeling, with a corner of her tongue between her teeth. Each card gets laid on the flagstone, squared, and tapped with a fingertip, as if she's setting a table for someone who hasn't yet decided to attend.

SOURCE. INVITATION. LIVING CLAIM.

I'm holding the first one open. It's heavier than the other two together. I can feel it in my boards: a great weight, patient and dry and slow, the weight of every sentence ever written pressing down on a single page. It's the whole book, leaning on me.

Permancer steps up to the edge of the threshold. He names the Count, once, in full. He names the source volume. He names the day of the first Jump. Then he closes the old invitation, the original one, the one that was written in good faith for a class of four, around the registered travellers, like a hand closing around a handful of coins. Dracula's name is outside it. It's the first time anyone has heard him not be a guest.

The new invitation waits at the returning fold. It's a small thing, hardly bigger than a calling card. It's been waiting there all evening.

Letters lift from the source. They come up off the page one at a time, black and quick, like a swarm of tiny insects, and catch at the hem of the Count's coat. He pulls back. Every borrowed handle in the room turns toward him, a hundred brass knobs, in a single soft clink.

They came off the page under my chin. I felt every one of them go.

“A technicality,” says the Count.

“You fitted through one,” says Penny.

She doesn't look up. She sets down the last of the three cards, at the corner of the threshold nearest Serenity, and leaves it there, face up, and steps back.

At the returning fold, Wicker's holding the last flap of paper between two fingers, exactly where he left it. He hasn't moved in a quarter of an hour.

The third card's for her.

nodes.title: Return by Ruse
nodes.body:
Dracula looks through the little window.

It's Wicker's, the paper room's, the one with the sill folded to the right height. It's standing at the threshold on a low table, a small square chamber made from spoiled menus and good intentions, and through its open window he can see the unwritten night: soft, open, the colour of a page before the ink gets to it.

“Unwritten,” says the Count.

Wicker stands beside the fold.

“Mostly.”

“You expect me to trust another gift?”

“I expect you to want the window.”

It's true. That's what's so unsettling about it. Wicker isn't lying. He isn't lying at all. There's not one false word in it. And it's *still* a trap. It's the cleverest, plainest, most honest trap I've ever seen a boy build, and he's built it with his own hands from a pile of old menus, in a single night, to give a vampire the one thing he wanted.

The Count enters.

He steps through the window, courteous and tall, stooping a little to fit. Wicker pulls the first fold.

It all goes at once. The window becomes a margin, a wide white margin with a faint ruled line down it. The floor tilts into a page. Dracula reaches for the door, and the handle's already ink, a long black smear that comes away on his glove. The room fills with the sound of a leaf turning: dry and soft and enormous.

I know that tilt. I'd know it anywhere. That's a book taking somebody back.

Serenity steps to the final edge.

“Wait.”

Wicker holds the fold. His knuckles go white. He's got the paper wound once round his hand, and the strain's coming up through it into his wrist, and his whole arm's trembling. He's holding up a *chapter* with a menu.

He waits.
nodes.braidText: The Count stepped into Wicker's paper room, and Wicker held the last fold for Serenity. She still held the living claim.

castMemories.memory: Wicker held the paper room's last fold with the Count inside it, his whole arm shaking, and waited for Serenity.
castMemories.aside: I held a chapter shut with a menu. My arm's still complaining. She said wait, so I waited.

storyScenes.title: The First Nightbound Morning
storyScenes.opening:
Morning finds Serenity in the Kitchens.

It's an ordinary morning. That's the astonishing thing about it. The light comes in at the windows in long dusty bars, and the pots hang in their rows like a ship's bells, and the whole room smells of toast and wet wool and last night's soup. Nothing's in the wrong place. Nothing's too quiet. The clocks, even the ones by the East Stacks, have all agreed, at last, on the hour.

She's built the toast tower again. It's got buttresses now. It's got a gargoyle, in the form of a very small burnt crust, and a little flag on top made out of a butter-wrapper, and it's about a foot taller than the one that fell down.

Sunlight crosses her hands. She's got a deck of cards, soft with age, and she's turning them over one at a time on the table. A moon. Another card: a moon. Another: a moon.

“Lazy,” she tells the deck.

Ambrose brings tea. He puts it down by her elbow without a word, and slides the sugar across, and goes away to find more toast.

On the lid of her map case, at the edge of the table, sits a small paper bird. It's been there since last night. It's got one wing folded flat and the other lifted, so that you can read the blue letters underneath, and she hasn't moved it. She hasn't turned it over. She's simply let it be there, the way you let a cat be on a chair.

Permancer arrives. He's carrying a phrase he's plainly been bringing all the way downstairs, carefully, like a full cup.

“Residual threshold sensitivity.”

Serenity looks up.

“Is that what the tea's called?”

He sits down. He's very tired. There's a crease in his waistcoat where he's slept in it.

“What would *you* call it?”

She doesn't answer at once. She looks, instead, at the pantry door. It's a low old door, painted green, and behind it there's a shelf of jars. And behind the jars, far too far away for anybody else to hear, is the sound she hasn't stopped hearing. Somewhere in the walls, a page turns.

She tilts her head. She listens.

“Nightbound,” she says.

It's a good word. It's a night-blue sort of word, with a cool edge and something in it that waits. It sits in the air over the table like a small, quiet bell.

Penny takes out a card. She holds her pencil over it, and she waits, as a clerk might wait, until Serenity nods.

I make room for the word too. I clear a space in my margin for it, a good wide one, the best I've got. It's the first time I've ever been asked to keep a word that wasn't written down by somebody else.

Permancer sets a new notice on the table, in his small cramped hand.

> Name every traveller. Close the list. Check both sides of the door.

Below that, underlined twice:

> No living anchors.

Serenity takes the pencil. She turns the notice towards herself. She writes, in a hand that's quick and sloping and not at all like his:

> Ask me before you make a map of what I can hear.

Permancer reads it. He reads it twice. Then he leaves it exactly where she wrote it, uncorrected, and sits back, and doesn't say another word.

Wicker appears in the doorway.

His hair's wet. He's evidently tried to improve it with water and lost. He's got ink to the wrist and a look of tremendous, careful lightness, like a man carrying a tray of glasses across an icy floor. He stops a good three feet from the table.

“May I?” he says.

Serenity turns a card face down. She does it slowly.

“Not today.”

He takes his hand off the door-frame.

nodes.title: The First Nightbound Morning
nodes.body:
Morning finds Serenity in the Kitchens.

It's an ordinary morning. That's the astonishing thing about it. The light comes in at the windows in long dusty bars, and the pots hang in their rows like a ship's bells, and the whole room smells of toast and wet wool and last night's soup. Nothing's in the wrong place. Nothing's too quiet. The clocks, even the ones by the East Stacks, have all agreed, at last, on the hour.

She's built the toast tower again. It's got buttresses now. It's got a gargoyle, in the form of a very small burnt crust, and a little flag on top made out of a butter-wrapper, and it's about a foot taller than the one that fell down.

Sunlight crosses her hands. She's got a deck of cards, soft with age, and she's turning them over one at a time on the table. A moon. Another card: a moon. Another: a moon.

“Lazy,” she tells the deck.

Ambrose brings tea. He puts it down by her elbow without a word, and slides the sugar across, and goes away to find more toast.

On the lid of her map case, at the edge of the table, sits a small paper bird. It's been there since last night. It's got one wing folded flat and the other lifted, so that you can read the blue letters underneath, and she hasn't moved it. She hasn't turned it over. She's simply let it be there, the way you let a cat be on a chair.

Permancer arrives. He's carrying a phrase he's plainly been bringing all the way downstairs, carefully, like a full cup.

“Residual threshold sensitivity.”

Serenity looks up.

“Is that what the tea's called?”

He sits down. He's very tired. There's a crease in his waistcoat where he's slept in it.

“What would *you* call it?”

She doesn't answer at once. She looks, instead, at the pantry door. It's a low old door, painted green, and behind it there's a shelf of jars. And behind the jars, far too far away for anybody else to hear, is the sound she hasn't stopped hearing. Somewhere in the walls, a page turns.

She tilts her head. She listens.

“Nightbound,” she says.

It's a good word. It's a night-blue sort of word, with a cool edge and something in it that waits. It sits in the air over the table like a small, quiet bell.

Penny takes out a card. She holds her pencil over it, and she waits, as a clerk might wait, until Serenity nods.

I make room for the word too. I clear a space in my margin for it, a good wide one, the best I've got. It's the first time I've ever been asked to keep a word that wasn't written down by somebody else.

Permancer sets a new notice on the table, in his small cramped hand.

> Name every traveller. Close the list. Check both sides of the door.

Below that, underlined twice:

> No living anchors.

Serenity takes the pencil. She turns the notice towards herself. She writes, in a hand that's quick and sloping and not at all like his:

> Ask me before you make a map of what I can hear.

Permancer reads it. He reads it twice. Then he leaves it exactly where she wrote it, uncorrected, and sits back, and doesn't say another word.

Wicker appears in the doorway.

His hair's wet. He's evidently tried to improve it with water and lost. He's got ink to the wrist and a look of tremendous, careful lightness, like a man carrying a tray of glasses across an icy floor. He stops a good three feet from the table.

“May I?” he says.

Serenity turns a card face down. She does it slowly.

“Not today.”

He takes his hand off the door-frame.

It's the whole of the exchange. There's nothing else in it. A boy at a door, and a girl at a table, and a single word, said without heat, and honoured at once.

“All right,” he says.

She watches him until he's gone. She keeps watching for a moment after. Then, with great deliberation, she reaches out and moves a piece of toast that was holding up the tower.

The tower falls. It falls slowly, in sections: gargoyle, buttress, flag. She laughs, once, at the mess, short and surprised.

“Terrible engineering.”

Ambrose brings more toast.

I want you to have a morning like this one. Not this one. One of yours.

storyScenes.title: Threshold Protocols
storyScenes.opening:
The Academy opened a door. Someone came through the other way.

By the Vault door there's a new notice, in Professor Permancer's small upright hand. It's been written in a single sitting, with a very good pen, and underlined at the bottom with a line so firm it's cut the paper.

1. Name the source and why you are entering it.
2. Name every traveller allowed to return.
3. Close the invitation around those names.
4. Check the doorway from both sides.
5. Leave the people in the source their own lives. No experiments on them for the sake of a lesson.
6. No living anchors.
7. Ask before using what a changed person can do.
8. After the return, check what came back different.

Penny's pinned the old list beside the new one. It's a short list, in the careful square print of a man who's been teaching it for eleven years. It's complete. That's why she kept it. It's perfectly good, and it's perfectly good for exactly the lesson it was written for, and it didn't have a single word in it about what to do when somebody asks to come back with you.

storyScenes.title: After the last lesson
storyScenes.opening:
Serenity is looking at two things on the table.

It's late. The Book Burrow's the warmest room in the Academy, a low round den under the roots of the library, lined with cushions and cracked spines and the smell of very old tea. It's a place for sitting in. Nobody's ever said that out loud, and nobody's ever needed to. A lamp's on in the corner. The two things lie in the little ring of its light.

One is Soren's folded bird.

The other is her repaired map case.

She opens the case. It's the first time she's looked at the repair properly. Wicker has put the new clasp on crooked. It sits a little off the true, a small bright slant of brass, and it closes *perfectly.* It closes with a clean small click, as though it had been made for her thumb alone.

“He knows I fasten it with one hand,” she says.

She says it to the lamp. She says it quite quietly, with a sort of wondering annoyance, like someone who's found a note in her own handwriting that she doesn't remember writing.

She closes it again, too hard.

“That doesn't help.”

I keep my ribbon still. I'm good at that, now. I've learned that there are conversations where the kindest thing a book can do is not turn a page.

“Soren asked about the glass roof,” she says. “A whole sentence, this time. With a question mark.”

She runs her thumb along the bird's wing. She does it slowly. The paper's gone soft there, from handling.

“I liked that.”

It's a plain sentence. She doesn't dress it up. She says it the way you'd say that you'd liked a day.

Outside, a pair of quills are arguing over which of them gets to be an arrow. It's a high, thin, cheerful squabble, the sort of noise a school makes when it's decided, against all the evidence, to be a school again.

She lets it go on for a while.

“And I still want to ask Wicker what he meant to happen,” she says. “Once I think I can bear listening.”

Her voice doesn't shake. It's more careful than that. It's the voice of someone setting a very full cup on a very small table.

She looks across the lamp at you.

“What would you do first?”

storyScenes.title: Go back once
storyScenes.opening:
Pick a sentence you've kept.

Go back to the thing it came from: the same window, the same cup, the same patch of path. Stand in front of it for a minute. Have another look.

Things don't hold still when you aren't watching. The light's moved. Somebody's put something down. You're a little different yourself: a day older, or a week, with a different mood on you. It's the same thing. It's never exactly the same.

Give me one sentence from this visit. It can have changed completely. It can be stubbornly, perfectly, comfortingly the same. Either one's a finding.

No first sentence yet? Keep one through Capture. Go back to its thing later. I'll wait here.

storyScenes.title: An evening in November
storyScenes.opening:
October's over. It didn't shut all its doors.

The Academy's gone back to its ordinary business. There are lessons again, and a timetable that holds, and a Quillquarium that's learned to splash downward. The stair between the supper tables is a stair in a book again, somewhere, and the paper moon is a moon on a page. But I keep finding October in odd places. A crumb in my gutter. A thorn between two leaves. A loose stitch in my spine that Penny still tells me, every morning, not to poke.

And I keep finding this.

Serenity made one plan before the last lesson. She did it quickly, on the back of a menu, in pencil, with her tongue between her teeth. She folded it small and gave it to me and said, “Keep that till I want it,” and I tucked it under my ribbon, where it sat for days without a word. I've been very careful with it. It's the first thing anyone's ever asked me to keep without telling me what it was.

Now I've found it again, flat and warm, with the creases soft from my keeping.

This is the page she picked first. First isn't forever.

nodes.title: The glass roof
nodes.body:
Rain has turned the glass roof into a second sky.

It comes down the panes in long running lines, thin and silver and wandering, a thousand tiny rivers racing each other down the slope. Beyond the glass it's dark. Inside, there's lamplight, one low lamp on the sill, and the smell of wet iron and warm tea and old paper, and the sound of the rain, which isn't a patter. It's a vast soft *rushing,* like the world turning over a page.

Soren's there already. He's sitting on the narrow bench under the highest pane, with two cups of tea beside him, steaming gently, and the paper bird in his lap. He hasn't written anything on its clean wing. I can see that from here. He's left it empty.

“You came,” he says.

He doesn't say it as if he'd doubted it. He says it as if he were reading it off a card he'd made himself.

“I said I would.” Serenity takes a cup. Her fingers fit around it as if it were hers. “That was the hard part of the conversation.”

He laughs. It's a short helpless laugh, the laugh of someone who's been caught off guard by his own happiness, and then, a second after, he catches himself looking at her neck.

She sees him do it.

“Ask,” she says.

“Does it hurt?”

“Not now.” She turns the cup in her hands. “Sometimes a closed book sounds like someone knocking from inside.”

Soren puts his cup down on the sill. He does it gently. He doesn't ask her to prove it. He doesn't say it must be awful. He just takes a breath, and lets it out, and says nothing at all, which is the best thing he could have said.

“I could go,” he says. “If you want it quiet.”

“The rain's loud enough to hide us both.”

It's a small thing to say. It's an invitation, in a way, and it's accepted before it's finished, like a hand taken. He settles back on the bench. A foot of dark wood lies between them. It isn't much. It's about the width of a map case.

You've carried me up the iron stair behind them. You hold me to the glass, and I press my corner to the pane. It's cold. It's very cold, and the rain's louder from this side, a great steady drumming that comes right through my boards and into the leaves. I can feel a hundred little rivers running down my cover. It's the first time I've been out in the rain.

Soren takes the bird out of his coat. It's still dry. It's perfectly folded, with its wings together and its small paper tail tucked, and he holds it in both hands as though it were alive.

Serenity's map case is at her feet. The crooked clasp catches the lamp.

She looks at you. Not at him: at you.

“What do I show him?”

Soren nods. He doesn't reach for the map. He sets the bird down on the bench by her hand, not on the paper, a careful two inches off, and he waits.

For a while neither of them says anything. It's a good silence. The rain does the talking.

When they go down, Soren gives her the bird.

He doesn't make a speech of it. He just holds it out, on the flat of his hand, in the doorway of the stair, and she takes it. She tucks it under the strap of her map case, outside, where the weather can get at it, not inside where it'd be safe. She does it deliberately. It's a choice, and I can tell it's one she's thought about.

The rain has made one wing soft. It's got a crease in it now, deep and silvery, the shape of a very small river.

I keep the crease. I take it into my memory as exactly as I can: the angle, the fold, the way the light lay in it.

Behind them, the glass roof goes on talking to itself in the dark.

nodes.title: At the table
nodes.body:
The Kitchens are empty except for a plate.

Ambrose has left it under a cloth at the middle of the long table. He's gone to bed, or pretends to have, and the lamps are low, and the fire's nearly out. A single copper pot gleams on its hook. Rain taps once at the window and thinks better of it.

Wicker sits at one end of the table. He's been there some time. He's brushed his hair, and got it wrong, and he's holding himself very straight, with his collar flat for once and his hands in plain view.

Serenity comes in and takes the other end.

It's a very long table. It's twenty feet of scrubbed pine, carved by three centuries of schoolchildren. She sets her map case down in the middle of it, in the exact centre, where neither of them can reach it without standing up.

“I thought one sentence could make him choose a harmless verb,” says Wicker.

“You wrote a way for him to choose.”

“I did.”

He keeps his hands flat on the table where she can see them. Usually he's got a joke ready before a hard word lands. He's got a joke for everything. I wait for one. It's the longest I've ever waited. Nothing comes.

“I was angry when you asked to take the anchor,” says Serenity. Her voice is level and low. “You kept trying to pay for it with yourself. If you'd done it, somebody else would have had to carry you home.”

“I know that now.”

“You knew I'd said no.”

“Yes.”

“You asked anyway.”

“Yes.”

The cloth on the plate lifts at one corner. A small wind's got into it, from nowhere. Under it, Ambrose has left two slices of pear tart, glazed and gold, on a blue-rimmed dish. Nobody reaches for them.

Wicker looks at the clasp. It's crooked, bright, and a little bent in the light of the lamp. He puts out a finger, as if to straighten it, and stops, and doesn't touch it.

“I can fix that.”

“It works.” She touches it once, with a single fingertip. “You can answer the question I came to ask. What will you do differently at the next door?”

He takes a breath. It takes him a long moment.

“Ask,” he says, “who has to live on the other side of it.”

It's a plain answer. It isn't clever. It's got no edge on it at all. It sits there on the table between them like a stone set down, and she looks at it for a good while.

She doesn't forgive him. She doesn't get up and leave, either. The tart sits between them. A log shifts in the grate.

You've set me down on the table, by the pear tart, and she turns her map over, to the blank back, and looks at you.
